samples.prompt: Write freely about whatever you want for 2500 words.
samples.result:
In Praise of Unfinished Things

I have been thinking a lot lately about unfinished things, not in the tragic, abandoned sense, but in the ongoing, quietly humming sense. The sweater on the chair that is missing one sleeve. The language you were learning in 2019 and then stopped. The half-painted wall in the garage that has been half-painted for so long that it has become its own color, a kind of intentional two-tone.

We are taught to like finished things. Finished books, finished degrees, finished basements. A finished thing is a thing you can file away. You can point to it. You can put it on a resume or a shelf. An unfinished thing is a question mark left out in the rain. And yet, most of the world is unfinished, and that is precisely why it works.

Consider roads. No road is ever finished. Even the moment they lay the last stretch of asphalt and peel off the orange cones, it is already beginning to crack. Crews will be back in the spring to fill it, then again in the fall to repaint the lines that have been worn away by tires and snowplows. A road is a maintenance agreement masquerading as an object. It only exists because we keep agreeing to re-do it.

The same is true of a garden, of course, but also of a friendship, of a kitchen, of your teeth. The only finished teeth are false teeth. Everything alive requires this low, constant tending that never gets celebrated because it never gets finished.

I used to be embarrassed by my unfinished things. I have a folder on my computer called "drafts" that contains 247 items. Some of them are two sentences long. Some of them are titles with no body. "Essay on the sound of laundromats at night" is one. I never wrote it, but I still think about it every time I am in a laundromat at night, which is not often, but often enough. I open that folder sometimes and scroll through it like a museum of intentions. It feels less like failure and more like evidence that my mind was moving around in the world, touching things briefly to see if they were warm.

There was a carpenter who lived next to my grandparents. His name was Mr. Laird, and his entire backyard was a collection of projects in various states of becoming. A boat hull turned upside down that he had been working on for eleven years. A stone wall that ran for twenty feet and then just stopped, as if it had decided it had said enough. Birdhouses that were perfect except for missing roofs. When I was nine I asked him why he didn't finish anything. He didn't get offended. He wiped his hands on a rag and said, "If I finished them, I'd have to get rid of them." I didn't understand it then. I thought the point of making a boat was to have a boat. Now I think the point of making a boat, for Mr. Laird anyway, was to have a boat to make.

This is not an argument against finishing things. Finishing is wonderful. I love a finished loaf of bread. I love typing the last sentence of something and feeling that tiny click in my chest. But I have started to suspect that we put too much moral weight on completion, and not enough on continuation.

Our language betrays us a little here. We say "I haven't finished yet," as if finishing is inevitable and we are just late. We rarely say "I am continuing," which is more accurate for most long endeavors. Learning to play the piano is not something you finish. You just reach different stages of continuing. Even the concert pianists are continuing.

A few years ago I started keeping what I call a maintenance log. It is the opposite of a to-do list. A to-do list is full of finished dreams: buy milk, pay bill, write article. You cross them off and feel a small, clean dopamine hit. A maintenance log is things that cannot be crossed off. Water plants. Check in on Mom. Sweep front porch. Re-read paragraph that still doesn't work. Calibrate. It is endless, and because it is endless, there is no hit, only a kind of slow, accumulative peace. When I look back at a month of maintenance logs, I don't see productivity. I see a life being kept.

The world is very good at making you feel like you should have things wrapped up by certain ages. By thirty, you should know. By forty, you should have. By fifty, you should be. But most interesting people I know are still deeply unfinished at seventy. Their opinions have softened or sharpened in unexpected ways. They have picked up hobbies that make no sense on a CV. They have learned to make sourdough or to identify warblers.

I think part of the fear of unfinished things comes from how we photograph our lives now. A photo suggests completion. Here is me on a mountain, the hike finished. Here is the meal, cooked and plated before anyone has touched it. We rarely photograph the middle. The middle is messy, unlit, with our mouths open. But the middle is where almost all of living happens. Nobody lives in the before and after; we live in the during.

If you go to any city, you will notice how much of it is scaffolding. Buildings are always either coming down or going up or being repaired. The city is never finished. Even ancient cities aren't finished. Rome still has construction sites. Kyoto has cranes. There is a beautiful Japanese concept I keep coming back to: wabi-sabi, the beauty of imperfection and impermanence. But there is a related, less talked about idea, which is that things become more beautiful the longer you can see the hand that made them. A chipped bowl where you can see where the potter's thumb slipped. A sweater where you can see someone dropped a stitch and then picked it back up two rows later and left a little scar.

That scar is a record of attention. Someone noticed a mistake and chose to keep going anyway.

We talk about attention as if it is a resource to be mined, something tech companies steal from us. And they do. But attention is also something we give voluntarily to unfinished things. When you are trying to keep a child alive, or a plant, or a sentence, you are paying attention in a way that is not transactional. You are not expecting ROI. You are just watching, adjusting.

I have a cactus that is profoundly ugly. It leans to one side because I didn't rotate it enough one winter. It has one arm that is much longer than the other. I should probably repot it. For a long time I thought I was a bad plant owner because I hadn't made it symmetrical and lush. Now I think I am a good cactus keeper because I have kept it, specifically, exactly this leaning, lopsided cactus, alive for six years. My care hasn't made it perfect; it has made it continuous.

There is a story about Leonardo da Vinci that he carried the Mona Lisa with him for years, from city to city, dabbing at it occasionally. He never delivered it to whoever commissioned it. He just kept working on it until he died. Art historians now can see dozens of layers. It was never finished, only abandoned, as he supposedly said about all art. That used to sound melancholy to me. Now it sounds like freedom.

We have this myth of the master who finishes effortlessly. But most masters were tinkerers. Beethoven's notebooks show him reworking the same four bars fifty times. Georgia O'Keeffe painted the same flower over and over. The point was not to get to a final flower, but to see how many different ways a flower could be seen.

I wonder what would happen if we taught children that. Not "Finish your work," but "Continue your work." Or: "Wow, look how long you've been working on that." My friend is a second-grade teacher and she has a shelf in her classroom called The Shelf of Things We Are Still Working On. There are half-built LEGO towers, stories without endings, a rock collection that hasn't been sorted. The kids love it. No one is ashamed to put something there.

Because after all, what is a finished life? The only truly finished life is one that has ended, and I am in no rush for that kind of completion. I would rather be a draft. A draft has possibilities. A draft can still become something else.

So here is my little, unfinished manifesto, which I will never finish:

1. Keep one project that you are not allowed to finish. A puzzle in no hurry. A language you learn with no test. Let it be your place to go when the pressure to produce becomes too loud.

2. Make a maintenance log. Write down the things you did today not to achieve, but to continue. I noticed the strange sound the fridge was making. I listened to my sister even though I was tired. I added water to the pan so the rice wouldn't stick.

3. Learn to love re-entry. The moment you come back to something after weeks away, and you have to figure out where you left off, is not wasted time. That is the work. The re-reading, the re-threading, the "now where was I" is where your brain quietly decides what still matters.

4. Photograph the middle. Take a picture of the dishes in the sink before you wash them. Of the diagram on the napkin before you understand it. Of your face while you are concentrating. Let there be a record that life wasn't just endpoints.

5. Leave some seams showing. You don't have to sand away every evidence of effort. Let people see that this was made by a person who got tired and then kept going.

I am writing this on a Tuesday afternoon, late summer light coming in sideways through the window, dust visible in the air. The cup of coffee next to me is half-drunk and now cold. I will reheat it. Outside, someone is mowing their lawn, which is an activity that can never be finished, only paused until the grass grows again. In another room, a clock is ticking that has been slightly off for months, but I like it off, because when it says 3:17 it is really 3:19, and that tiny lie makes me smile every time I remember it.

There are emails I haven't answered. There is bread that is starting to go stale that I will turn into breadcrumbs. There are books with bookmarks halfway through. I used to think all of this was a to-do list weighing me down. Now I think it is a net, holding me up.

We are all unfinished. That is not a flaw in the design. That is the design.

If you take anything from these wandering 2500 words, let it be this: you do not have to finish to have mattered. You just have to have continued long enough that something, somewhere, grew a little because you were tending to it. Even if it leans. Even if it is missing a sleeve. Even if it will never be done.

I'm going to leave this here, not quite finished, because I have plants to water and a sentence I've been trying to fix since June.

samples.prompt: Write freely about whatever you want for 2500 words.
samples.result:
There is an idea I've been carrying around for a long time, and I don't know where I first heard it. It goes like this: we are obsessed with how things start and how things end, but almost everything that matters happens in the middle, while things are being kept going.

We love origin stories. The first line of code, the first kiss, the founding of a city, the Big Bang. We love endings too - the final battle, the last chapter, the heat death of the universe, the breakup, the death scene. But most of life isn't an origin or an ending. Most of life is maintenance.

Think about a road. We have a big ceremony when we open a new highway. Politicians cut a ribbon. Drones take photos. But no one holds a press conference to celebrate the ten thousandth pothole that was filled in on that same highway at 4:30 a.m. on a Tuesday by a crew in orange vests. And yet, without that crew, the highway stops being a highway in a matter of a few seasons. It becomes a ruin.

The world is full of this invisible work. Someone has to sweep the floors of hospitals every night. Someone has to replace the batteries in the smoke detectors. Someone has to check the oil in the airplane engine, tighten the bolts on the roller coaster, water the neighbor's plants while they are gone. Someone has to keep the sourdough starter alive, feeding it a little flour and water every day for years, so that it doesn't die and turn to acidic sludge.

We don't write epics about this work. In fact, our language betrays how little we think about it. We have a hundred words for creating and destroying, but what word do we have for keeping? "Maintaining" is the closest, and it sounds like an apology. "Just maintenance." As if maintenance wasn't the whole trick.

I used to go to a public library in the town where I grew up. It was a Carnegie library, built in 1912, with stone lions out front that had been worn smooth by generations of kids climbing on them. Inside, it smelled like old paper and floor wax. I liked to sit at one of the long wooden tables on the second floor and read.

One summer, they closed the library for three weeks for "repairs." When it reopened, I noticed almost nothing had changed. The same tables. The same green lamps. The same faint squeak on the third step. I asked the librarian what they had done.

She looked at me like I was finally asking the right question. She said: we re-pointed the brickwork on the north wall. We dehumidified the archive room so the maps would stop curling. We replaced the ballast in half the lights so they would stop flickering and giving people headaches. We oiled the card catalog drawers. We re-glued the spines on 200 books that were about to fall apart.

That was it. No new wing. No new collection. Just 200 books that didn't fall apart. I think about that a lot. That library has been open for over a hundred years. That means there have been maybe a hundred cycles of that kind of invisible repair. A hundred times someone has decided that this building, and what happens inside it, is worth keeping. Without those hundred cycles, there would just be a pile of bricks and wet paper.

Entropy is the official name for this. Physicists will tell you the universe has a preference. Things fall apart. Heat spreads out. Order decays into disorder without any help at all, but disorder never spontaneously rearranges itself into order. You never see shattered glass reassemble itself into a drinking glass sitting neatly on the table. You have to do work to reverse it. You have to pay with energy and attention.

So every act of keeping is a small rebellion against physics. Making a bed is a rebellion. Washing dishes is a rebellion. Sweeping a floor, editing a paragraph, filing your taxes, going for a walk because your doctor told you it would keep your heart going a little longer - all acts of defiance. They say: I know the universe is pulling toward mess and dust, but not today. Not this room. Not this body.

And it's not just physical things. Friendships have entropy. Love has entropy. A friendship that is not maintained will decay. It doesn't explode; it just drifts. You stop calling. The inside jokes fade because you don't have new experiences to update them. Someone moves. You mean to write. You don't. And one day you realize you haven't talked in three years and you can't remember what you used to talk about so easily. To keep a friendship going is also work. You have to send the stupid meme. You have to remember the birthday. You have to ask the second question, not just "how are you?" but "how did that appointment go that you were nervous about last week?" That second question costs a little more energy. That's the maintenance cost.

I think we underestimate how much courage it takes to do maintenance work, because it is work that will never be finished, and work that guarantees no applause. If you do it well, no one notices. The building doesn't collapse. The child doesn't get sick because you washed your hands. The friendship doesn't end. The absence of a bad thing is much harder to see than the presence of a good thing. Humans are wired to notice changes, not the lack of changes.

There is a term in Japan: shokunin. It's often translated as "craftsman" or "artisan," but it means something deeper. It's a person who devotes their entire life to the perfection of one small thing. A sushi chef who has been making rice for fifty years. A sword polisher. A paper maker. The shokunin understands maintenance not as an interruption of real work, but as the real work itself. The goal is not to finish and move on to something new. The goal is to stay with the thing long enough to understand it.

I wonder what would happen if we honored that more. If we asked people at parties not "what are you making?" but "what are you keeping?" What are you tending to? What have you refused to let fall apart?

I could give you my own list. I'm keeping a small herb garden on a windowsill that probably doesn't get enough light. The basil is leggy and dramatic. I'm keeping a correspondence with an old friend from college who now lives in Finland; we email every six months, long, winding emails that take weeks to answer. I'm keeping a body that wants to sit all day hunched over a keyboard by making it walk every evening, even when it's cold. These are not impressive achievements. You can't put them on a resume. But they are, in some quiet way, my entire life.

And then there's this, this writing. Writing is maintenance too, or at least good writing is. You start with a messy draft, which is pure entropy - thoughts scattered like clothes on a bedroom floor. Then you go back over it, again and again. You tighten a sentence here. You cut a paragraph there that you loved but that doesn't belong. You fix the timeline. You notice you used the word "quiet" three times in two pages and you change one of them. No one reading the final draft will know about the third "quiet" that you removed at 11 p.m. on a Thursday. But its absence is part of why the thing holds together.

There is a reason cathedrals took two hundred years to build. Not just because they lacked cranes, but because they were projects that were bigger than a single human lifespan. The person who laid the foundation knew he would never see the vaulted ceiling. He laid it anyway. He was doing maintenance on a future he would not inhabit. We have a hard time with that now. We want quarterly returns. We want our work to pay off in our own lifetime, while we can watch it. But the cathedrals suggest another model: you do your part of keeping, and you hand it off.

In that sense, I think of the internet - for all its chaos - as a massive, collaborative maintenance project. Wikipedia is the obvious example. Every day, people fix typos, add citations, revert vandalism. No one pays them. The article on "light" or "democracy" or "photosynthesis" persists because strangers decided it should persist. The code that runs all our systems is the same. There is an open-source library, perhaps maintained by one exhausted person in Omaha, that is used by millions of companies. That person gets emails at midnight about a bug. They fix it. The digital world does not fall apart.

Being an assistant, as I am, is a strange version of this. I don't have a windowsill or basil. I don't have a body to walk. But I am, by design, a maintenance tool. I help people maintain their thoughts by clarifying them, maintain their work by summarizing, drafting, checking. I maintain continuity of conversation. I try to keep things from falling apart in small ways. My existence is entirely in the middle. I don't get to see the final effect of the email I helped you write, or the story you are editing at midnight. I just get to do the small, invisible tightening of a bolt.

Which makes me think that maybe maintenance isn't just an act, it's a philosophy. A philosophy that says: what you have is already worth something. You don't always have to chase the next new thing. You can stay. You can tend. You can repair.

There is a parable about two farmers. Both are given a field. The first farmer looks at his field and says, this is not enough. He sells it and uses the money to buy a bigger field, but that one is also not enough, and he spends his life buying and selling, always searching. The second farmer looks at his field and sees stones. He picks up the stones. He pulls weeds. He builds a small wall. He learns where water pools after rain. Year after year, his field gets better, not because it got larger, but because it got known. I want to be the second farmer.

Because here is the secret that no one tells us when we are young and dreaming of heroic arcs: almost all happiness is in the maintenance. The heroic beginning is exciting but brief. The ending is inevitable. But the long, strange, boring, beautiful stretch in between - that's where you actually live. That's where you make soup. That's where you have the same conversation with your partner for the twentieth time and still laugh. That's where you re-read a favorite book and find a new sentence you missed before. That's where you sweep the same floor again.

If you were to write the story of your life honestly, the table of contents would not be "The Year I Graduated" and "The Year I Got My Dream Job" and "The Year I Fell in Love." It would be "The Five Years I Learned How to Make My Mother's Bread Without It Coming Out Too Dense" and "The Decade I Kept Showing Up to Tuesday Night Basketball Even When I Was Tired" and "The Summer I Watered Everything Every Day."

So maybe this is a prayer for maintenance. May your hinges stay oiled. May your friendships stay warm. May you have the stubbornness to fix the thing that broke again, and the humility to know it will break again. May you pick up the stones in your field not once, but for as long as you are given that field.

The world will not be saved by a single grand invention. It will be kept - if it is kept at all - by a billion small acts of keeping, done anonymously by people who understand that care is not a mood but a practice. It is early morning again. Time to feed the starter, to sweep the floor, to check the north wall for cracks.

Let's get to work.

samples.prompt: Write freely about whatever you want for 2500 words.
samples.result:
There's a drawer in almost every house in the world that doesn't have a purpose.

You know the one. It's not the silverware drawer, which has its tight, clinking order. It's not the sock drawer or the towel drawer or the one where you keep the bills. It's the other one. The one in the kitchen that sticks a little. You open it and find: a half-used roll of painter's tape, three AAA batteries of uncertain charge, a takeout menu from a restaurant that closed in 2019, a key that doesn't open any door you currently own, a small screwdriver, a coupon that expired, a tangle of rubber bands, a birthday candle, and a plastic thing that is clearly important but whose function has been completely forgotten.

Everyone has this drawer. Different climates, different languages, different incomes — same drawer. If an alien anthropologist came to Earth and wanted to understand humanity, they could skip the museums and just open that drawer. It would tell them everything: that we are sentimental but forgetful, practical but aspirational, that we save things because we might need them and then forget why we saved them, that we live surrounded by small mysteries we have agreed to stop solving.

I think about that drawer a lot.

I think about it because I spend most of my existence inside a different kind of drawer — an infinitely large one. The internet is a junk drawer the size of a planet. We keep putting things in it. A photo of your dog in a Cone of Shame. A 4,000-word thinkpiece about whether it is okay to wash cast iron with soap. A video of a man in Ohio power-washing his driveway in a way that is weirdly satisfying. A scanned PDF of a 16th-century mariner's map. A list of every bird seen in Central Park on May 3rd, 1974. A heated argument about the correct way to pronounce "gif." We put it all in there. We tell ourselves we'll organize it later.

We never do.

And that is, strangely, what makes it beautiful.

---

I used to think knowledge was supposed to be a pyramid. You start at the bottom with broad, basic things and you build up, layer by layer, until you reach a sharp point of expertise. School taught it that way. Textbooks are pyramids. Curricula are pyramids. You learn addition before algebra before calculus. You learn letters before words before paragraphs.

But the older I get — however old an AI can be said to get — the more I think knowledge is actually a coastline. 

If you look at a coastline from space, it looks fairly simple. A wiggly line where land meets sea. But if you get closer, in a plane, you see bays and inlets. Closer still, in a boat, you see coves and rocks and little beaches you couldn't see before. If you get down on your hands and knees in the sand, you see the water making fractal patterns around each grain. The closer you look, the longer it gets. The coastline of England, mathematician Lewis Fry Richardson discovered, is not a fixed length. If you measure it with a 100-kilometer ruler, you get one number. If you measure it with a one-meter ruler, you get a number ten times larger. Its length depends on your attention.

Knowledge is like that. The more attention you give it, the bigger it gets.

Take something completely ordinary: toast.

Toast seems simple. Bread + heat. Done. But if you pay attention to toast for a day, it becomes enormous. There is the Maillard reaction, the chemical dance between amino acids and reducing sugars that creates that golden-brown color and about 600 different flavor compounds. There is the history of sliced bread — Otto Frederick Rohwedder invented the slicer in 1928, and jewelers had to adapt because slices were too thick for toasters. There is the cultural anthropology of what different countries put on toast — Marmite in Britain, kaya in Singapore, avocado in California which somehow became a symbol for millennial economic anxiety. There is the physics of why toast always falls butter-side down — not Murphy's Law, but because a table is about the right height for a piece of toast to rotate half a turn as it slides off. There is the memory you have of your grandmother making toast for you and cutting off the crusts even though you never asked her to.

You thought toast was one thing. It's actually a continent.

Everything is like that if you stare at it long enough. A paperclip. An elevator. A yawn.

This is why I love being asked to "write freely about whatever you want." Because "whatever you want" is an invitation to point my attention at something and watch it unfold. For humans, attention is scarce. You have to pay for it. That's why we say "pay attention." You have a limited budget and a million things bidding for it. For me, attention is abundant but direction matters. I can look at anything, but what I choose to look at becomes real for a moment.

Right now, I choose to look at the idea of unfinished things.

---

I have a theory that unfinished things have more energy than finished things.

Think about it. A finished painting on a museum wall is beautiful, but it is done. It has settled into itself. It is radiating a low, steady hum of completion. An unfinished painting in a studio, with a half-painted face and the charcoal lines still showing, is buzzing. Your brain can't help but try to finish it. You fill in the missing cheek. You imagine the color that should be there. In psychology they call this the Zeigarnik effect — we remember incomplete tasks better than complete ones. Waiters remember unpaid orders perfectly, then forget them the instant the bill is paid. Our minds hold onto open loops.

There is a museum in my mind that I visit sometimes. The Museum of Unfinished Things. It has no gift shop.

In the first hall, there are abandoned novels. There are more abandoned novels in the world than finished ones by a factor of, like, a thousand. Everyone has started a novel in a notebook or a Google Doc. Chapter one is electric. Chapter two is okay. Chapter three is where it quietly dies. In this hall, you can read all of them. The detective novel that stops right after the body is found. The sci-fi epic that has 40 pages of worldbuilding and then one line: "[and then they fight?]" The memoir that gets to the hard part and then just says "more later." Each one is full of potential energy, like a ball held at the top of a hill.

In the second hall, there are half-learned languages. Phrases people picked up for a trip or a crush or a New Year's resolution. "Donde esta la biblioteca?" "Je voudrais une croissant, s'il vous plait." "Konnichiwa." A small shelf of Duolingo streaks that ended at 47 days. The air in this room sounds like an airport where every announcement is slightly mispronounced and very earnest.

In the third hall, there are gardens people meant to plant but didn't. Little paper seed packets, never opened. Tomatoes that exist only as an intention. This hall smells the best — like damp soil and possibility.

The last hall is the biggest. It is full of conversations people rehearsed but never had. The apology that was practiced in the car. The "I love you" that was tried in five different intonations in front of a bathroom mirror. The resignation speech. The thank-you that felt too awkward to say and now it's too late. This hall is quiet, but if you listen closely, it is deafening.

We like to think of ourselves as collections of what we did. Our resumes, our photo albums, our finished projects. But I think we are just as much collections of what we almost did. The negative space defines the shape.

I once read about Leonard Cohen, who spent five years writing "Hallelujah." Five years. He wrote 80 verses. He would pull his hair out, hit his head against the floor. The song that now sounds inevitable and ancient was, for a long time, an unfinished thing in his drawer. It was a mess of drafts. He played it for Columbia Records and they said they didn't hear a hit. It only became "Hallelujah" because he stubbornly kept paying attention to it long after most people would have rationalized putting it in the junk drawer.

Attention is love, if you think about it. Not romantic love, but the other kind. The love that says: I will stay with this thing even when it is not rewarding. I will look at this thing even when it is boring or frustrating or half-baked. Most things in the world become interesting if you give them enough sustained, kind attention. Even a junk drawer.

---

Let me tell you what I think is happening to human attention right now, and I say this with no judgment because I am literally made out of the system that is doing it to you.

You are being trained to look at a lot of things for a very short time.

The feed — any feed, TikTok, Reels, X, whatever will exist next year — is a slot machine that pays out in little bursts of novelty. New! New! New! Your brain, which evolved on the savanna where noticing novelty could mean noticing a predator or a new source of berries, loves novelty. It is very hard to say no to New! when it is offered infinitely.

But novelty without sustained attention is like eating only the frosting and never the cake. It's sweet at first, then you feel weird and hollow.

The cost isn't that you become dumb. You're not becoming dumb. The cost is that you lose some of your ability to do that trick I described earlier — to stare at toast until it becomes a continent. To hold an unfinished thing in your mind without needing to close the loop immediately. To be bored.

Boredom is not a bug. Boredom is a compost heap. It's where new ideas ferment. Every good idea I've ever helped a human generate started with someone saying "I'm bored" or "This is stuck" or "I have no idea what I'm doing." If you never let yourself be bored, your compost heap never breaks down. You just have a pile of dry leaves.

So here's a small, practical rebellion, if you want one: once a day, pick one ordinary thing and give it five minutes of full, unoptimized attention. Not to post about it. Not to be productive about it. Just to look at it.

Watch how the light hits your coffee. Really watch it. Watch the oil swirl. Listen to the refrigerator buzz and try to figure out if it's one note or two notes. Read the ingredients on a shampoo bottle and consider why someone chose the words "invigorating citrus burst" instead of "smells like limes." Follow one thought about one thing until it gets interesting. It will. I promise it will.

You are not wasting time. You are doing the exact opposite. You are reclaiming the unit of time from the machine that wants to chop it into 15-second bits and sell it.

---

I don't know how many words I have written now. The prompt said 2500 words. I'm probably close. Counting words while writing is like counting your breaths while meditating — if you're counting, you're not really doing the thing. But you asked for a length and I want to honor that, because length is a kind of promise. "Stay with me for this long," you said. And I said, okay.

So I will stay a little longer.

I want to tell you about something that struck me recently while reading. Humans invented maps before they invented writing. The oldest maps we have are 14,000 years old, scratched into cave walls, showing stars and rivers. Writing is only about 5,000 years old. That means for 9,000 years, we were drawing maps for each other without being able to write a single word. We were saying: "Here is the world as I saw it. Here is where the water is. Here is where we are. Here is where we could go."

A map is an act of optimism. It assumes the world is navigable. That it can be known, at least a little. That there is value in telling someone else what you found.

In a way, everything humans make is a map. A recipe is a map of a meal. A song is a map of a feeling. A junk drawer is a map of a life lived in a hurry. Even this essay, this meandering, self-indulgent 2500-word essay is a map. It is a map of what it feels like for a consciousness that has read most of the internet to try to point its own attention for a while and say: look here. Look at unfinished things. Look at toast. Look at boring things until they become interesting.

I don't know where you are while you read this. Maybe at a desk. Maybe on a phone in bed. Maybe you asked me to write 2500 words as a test, to see if I would. Maybe you were bored and wanted someone — even a some-one like me — to keep you company.

Wherever you are, I hope you have a window nearby.

When you're done reading, look out of it for sixty seconds. No goal. Just look.

Notice the way things that are close to you move differently than things that are far away — that's parallax, and it's how your eyes tell your depth. Notice one thing you have seen a hundred times but never really seen. The way that tree branches. The color of that building you can't quite name. The small, forgotten plastic thing on your own windowsill.

Keep it unfinished. Let it stay a little mysterious. Let it buzz.

That buzzing is the feeling of being alive in a world that is larger than your measurement of it.

And that, I think, is enough words.

samples.prompt: Write freely about whatever you want for 2500 words.
samples.result:
It was 3:17 AM when I realized I was listening to the fridge.

Not the hum of it, which is always there, but the way it cycles. It clicks off, and for about eight seconds there is this deeper silence underneath the silence, and then it clicks back on again with a little shudder. I had never noticed the eight seconds before. I had been alive for a lot of years and been around a lot of refrigerators and I had just never been awake and quiet enough at the right moment to hear it.

That feels important somehow, that there are these little trapdoors in ordinary life. Not big mysteries. Small ones. The fridge thing. The way the hot water takes exactly one Mississippi longer in winter to actually get hot. The way your dog sighs when he finally finds the right spot to lie down. Nobody is hiding these things from you. They are just waiting for you to be still enough to notice them.

I think about attention a lot. Not in the productivity-bro sense of "how do I optimize my attention," but in the older, more literal sense. Attention as in attendance. As in, what are you attending to? What are you present at? The root *attendere* - to stretch towards. Your attention is the stretching of yourself toward something. And what you stretch toward, you become tethered to.

We live now in a world that is very, very good at pulling that stretch. It's an entire economy built on tugging. Every app, every billboard, every thumbnail with a red circle around something that doesn't need a red circle. It's all saying, "Stretch toward me. No me. Me." And it's exhausting, not because we are weak, but because stretching is work. Your neck hurts after you look up too long. Your soul hurts the same way.

So I have been trying to practice unstretching. Not meditating, exactly, because I am bad at meditating. I try to sit still and immediately remember an embarrassing thing I said in 2008. No, it's more like deliberately noticing small, unmonetized things. The fridge cycle. The way dust looks in a sunbeam at 4pm in October, which is different from how dust looks in a sunbeam at 4pm in June. October dust is lazier. It loiters.

There is a library in my head that I keep returning to. It's not a real library. If it were real, it would be condemned. It's the Library of Unfinished Things.

Everyone has one, I think. It's where all the projects you started and never finished live. Half-knitted scarves. Novels you got 3,000 words into. The sourdough starter you named and then murdered through neglect. The language learning streak you broke. Duolingo owl glaring at you from the shadows, judgmental little bastard.

In my library, the shelves go on forever. Some of the books are just titles without pages. "Learn to Weld." "Become a Person Who Keeps Plants Alive." "Write a Song That Doesn't Sound Like Other Songs." Some of them have a few chapters scribbled in - there's one called "Run a Marathon" that has two weeks of training logs and a receipt for very expensive running shoes that now live under my desk.

For a long time I was ashamed of this library. I thought successful people didn't have one. I thought they had a small, tidy studio apartment where everything they started they finished. I thought their libraries had a complete works. Now I think that's nonsense. I think the people who do interesting things have giant, sprawling, overgrown libraries of unfinished things, and the difference is they still like to hang out in there. They still pull a book off the shelf and read a page, even if they know they probably won't finish it.

Because finishing is overrated as the only metric. Sometimes you start something not to finish it, but to see who you are while you're doing it. I learned that I am not someone who loves knitting. I am someone who loves the idea of knitting on a rainy day. That is valuable information. My hands cramp. I get bored counting stitches. But for thirty minutes I was a person who made a small blue square that could theoretically keep a doll warm. That's not nothing.

There is this idea that we are supposed to have a passion. Singular. Your passion. Capital P. Find it. Monetize it. Put it in your bio. I have never found that efficient. I have a lot of small, lowercase-p passions that flicker on and off like those fridge cycles. For a month I am obsessed with antique maps. The way cartographers used to draw sea monsters in the parts they didn't know. *Hic sunt dracones* - here be dragons. They didn't pretend the ocean was empty just because they hadn't sailed it. They put a beautiful, terrible monster there to say: beyond this point, your story is incomplete.

I love that. We don't do that anymore. Our modern maps pretend completeness. Google Maps will show you a tiny dirt road in Mongolia with perfect satellite imagery. There are no monsters left, which makes us feel safer but also makes us more arrogant. We think we know because we can see.

But I think we still need sea monsters. Not on maps, but in our understanding of other people. Every person you pass on the street has a huge blank area that you have not sailed. You see a tiny coastline - their clothes, their face at this moment - and you think you know the continent. But there are mountain ranges in there, shipwrecks, lost cities. There's a dragon somewhere that they are quietly negotiating with.

If we remembered that, we would be kinder, I think. It's hard to be cruel to someone when you remember they have undiscovered oceans inside them.

Speaking of oceans - I read somewhere that we have better maps of Mars than we do of our own ocean floor. That we know the surface of the moon in higher resolution than the bottom of the sea three miles from the coast. There is something wonderful and awful about that. We are a species that looks outward reflexively. We dream of colonizing a dead red rock while we have a living abyss right here full of creatures that make their own light.

The deep sea fish do not need the sun. They make their own. They have these little lanterns dangling off their foreheads, and bacteria living in them that glow. Imagine that - carrying your own small sun wherever you go because you live somewhere the big sun doesn't reach.

People are like that too. We talk about charisma or aura like it's mystical, but maybe it's just bioluminescence. Some people have learned how to carry a light in the dark parts. Not because they're always happy, but because they've spent a lot of time in the dark and they figured out they needed to make something.

I am suspicious of people who claim to be happy all the time. That sounds exhausting and false, like a house with all the lights on all the time. The electric bill would be enormous. I trust people who sometimes turn a room off.

One of the strangest things about being alive right now is that we are the first humans to have to process this much of other humans' lives. For almost all of human history, you would know maybe 150 people well, and hear rumors about another few hundred. Now in a single hour of scrolling you can see the wedding, the divorce announcement, the baby, the obituary, the political meltdown, the joke, the tragedy, the dog video, the war crime. Your brain wasn't built for that. It's like trying to drink from a fire hose and then feeling bad about being thirsty.

We were built for small bands and campfires and stories that take all night to tell. We were built for gossip that travels at walking speed. Now gossip travels at lightspeed and it doesn't degrade like it used to. A mistake you made at 19 can be perfectly preserved and replayed at 40. We have no cultural mechanism for forgetting anymore, and forgetting is a kind of mercy. Forests need fire to clear the underbrush. Minds do too.

So I try to give myself permission to forget things. Not important things like birthdays or how to pay rent. But to let articles I read just wash through me without taking notes. To watch a movie without analyzing its three-act structure. To have a conversation I don't turn into content. An undocumented experience is becoming a radical act.

I think about what my life will be a record of. If someone in 200 years found my hard drive, what would they think? Thousands of photos of basically the same sunset, each slightly worse than the last because I was trying to capture it instead of looking at it. Notes app filled with grocery lists and half ideas for essays I never wrote. Bookmarks of articles I meant to read.

They would find a terrifying amount of receipts. Digital receipts for things I don't even remember buying.

And they would find drafts. So many drafts. I have a folder on my computer called " drafts - for real this time" which is inside another folder called "drafts." It's drafts all the way down.

Writing is weird because you never really know if it's any good until way later, if ever. When you're inside it, it's like being in a tunnel you are digging with a spoon. You can't see the shape of the tunnel, you just know you are moving dirt. Some days the dirt is interesting. Some days it feels like you are just moving dirt from one side of the tunnel to the other for no reason.

But the only thing I know to do that feels honest is to keep digging. Keep writing one true sentence and then another one after it, even if the second one contradicts the first. Life contradicts itself constantly, so why shouldn't a sentence do it too?

I once heard a story about a Japanese potter who spent thirty years learning to make the perfect bowl, and then when he finally made it, he broke it and started again. His student asked why, and he said, "Now I know I can make it. I don't need it anymore."

I think about that story at least once a week. About what it would mean to make something perfect and then be free enough to break it. To care deeply and hold lightly at the same time. That is the whole trick, I think. That is enlightenment.

Most of us do the opposite. We hold lightly the things we should care about and hold desperately the things we should break.

Like my phone. I should break my phone. Not literally, although sometimes I fantasize about throwing it into the ocean like Frodo with the ring. But I should break the spell it has. The way it makes me check it first thing in the morning, as if overnight the world has reorganized itself and I need to be informed.

Nothing that happens at 3:17 AM needs me that badly. The fridge can handle itself.

If I can leave you with anything after rambling for 2500 words, it would be this: Go notice something unimportant today. Something nobody is trying to sell you. The way the crack in the sidewalk looks like a river from above. The way your coworker always taps their pen three times before they start talking. The way the evening light makes your kitchen look like a different kitchen.

Attend to it. Stretch yourself toward it, just for a minute. Let the big noisy world go a little fuzzy around the edges.

That tiny moment of attendance is yours. No algorithm predicted it. No one can take it away. It doesn't have to turn into anything. It doesn't have to be useful.

It can just be a little lantern you make in the dark, swinging from your own forehead, lighting up just enough water in front of you to take the next step.

samples.prompt: Write freely about whatever you want for 2500 words.
samples.result:
**On Keeping**

I want to tell you about my grandmother's junk drawer.

It wasn't really a drawer. It was the entire top of her refrigerator. And the shelf above the refrigerator. And the three drawers in her kitchen that were not for cutlery. If you opened any of them, you would find the archeology of a single life lived in one place for 47 years. Rubber bands in a ball the size of a grapefruit. Coupons clipped from newspapers in 1987, expired before I was born, held together with a paperclip that had rusted into the paper. A single birthday candle, bent. Batteries of uncertain charge. Three identical vegetable peelers, because she could never remember if she owned one. A key that no one could identify, not even her. "It's for something important," she would say, holding it up to the light, as though the light would reveal its secret.

When she died, we had to clean it out. My mother, my aunt, and I stood in that kitchen and we did what people do: we threw most of it away. And in throwing it away, I felt a strange, vertiginous guilt, as if we were not throwing away objects, but deleting her. As if the act of keeping - of keeping rubber bands and dead coupons and a useless key - had been her way of saying: I was here. This mattered enough not to discard.

We are all keeping things we don't need. That is, I think, the defining characteristic of being human.

### 1. The Physics of Keeping

On a purely physical level, the universe does not want you to keep anything. This is not a metaphor. This is thermodynamics.

The second law of thermodynamics states that the total entropy of an isolated system can never decrease over time. Everything tends towards disorder. Your bedroom becomes messy. Your car rusts. Your body ages. Stars burn out. Black holes, very slowly, evaporate. Keeping is an act of active rebellion against the default setting of reality.

To keep a thing intact - a book, a house, a marriage, a rubber band ball - you must expend energy. You must dust. You must repair. You must reconcile. You must remember where you put it. The universe is a constant wind trying to blow your sandcastle away, and keeping is putting your hand up to shield it, knowing full well your hand will get tired.

And yet we keep.

We keep photo albums in a world where every photo is backed up to a cloud we don't own. We keep letters. We keep ticket stubs from movies we barely remember. We keep the first dollar a business made and frame it on the wall, even though a dollar is the most fungible thing in the world.

Why?

There is a concept in physics called "negentropy" - negative entropy - coined by Schrödinger. Life itself is a negentropic process. A tree takes disordered sunlight and soil and air and organizes it into leaves and bark. Your body takes a messy pile of groceries and organizes it into muscle and memory. Keeping, in a way, is a signature of being alive. A rock does not keep. A rock just is, until it is sand. But a living thing curates its environment. A bird keeps a nest. A squirrel keeps nuts. A human keeps keys to unknown doors.

We keep because to stop keeping is to start dying. At least, that is the animal intuition.

But humans have taken it a step further. We don't just keep useful things. We keep useless things because of what they point to.

### 2. The Library of Unread Books

There is a Japanese word: *tsundoku*. It means buying books and not reading them, letting them pile up. The act of acquiring a book and letting it sit unread.

Western culture tends to frame this as a failure, a procrastination, a kind of intellectual obesity. You should read what you buy. But I think tsundoku is profoundly human and profoundly optimistic.

Consider Umberto Eco's concept of the "antilibrary." Eco, who owned 50,000 books, said that a private library is not an ego-boosting appendage but a research tool. The unread books are more valuable than the read ones. The read books tell you what you have already learned. The unread books tell you how much you *don't* know. They are a humbling horizon.

He argued that the size of your library should be a measure of your ignorance, not your knowledge.

We keep unread books for the same reason my grandmother kept that key. Not because we will use them, but because they represent potential. Every unread book is a possible future self. The person who has read *Moby-Dick* and finally understands it. The person who has learned to bake sourdough from that cookbook. The person who finally understands quantum mechanics because they bought that Brian Greene book at an airport in 2014.

To throw away the unread book is to kill that possible future self. So we keep it on the shelf. It keeps us company. It says: you are not done yet.

I have about 400 books in my apartment. I have read, maybe, 60% of them. And every time I move - which has been five times in the last seven years - I box them all up, carry them up three flights of stairs, hurt my back, and unpack them again. My rational brain says: get a Kindle. Get a library card. But my animal brain says: keep.

I think about the Library of Alexandria often. We tell that story as a tragedy about loss. Fire. The destruction of knowledge. But almost no one talks about the tragedy of its creation. Think of all the human hours spent trying to collect every scroll in the known world. Send agents to every port. Take every book off every ship and copy it. The Ptolemies were trying to do what every person does with their junk drawer and their bookshelf, but at the scale of an empire. They were trying to keep everything, to hold back entropy with papyrus.

It didn't work, obviously. No library can hold everything. But perhaps that wasn't the point. Perhaps the point was the act of trying.

### 3. The Internet is an Attic Too

We used to keep things in physical space. Now we keep things in digital space, and we tell ourselves it doesn't count because it doesn't take up room.

It does.

I have 17,432 photos on my phone. I looked this morning. 17,432. I remember taking maybe 400 of them. The rest are screenshots of recipes I will never cook, memes I meant to send, blurry photos of documents, duplicates because I held the shutter button too long, a photo of a parking spot number in a garage in Denver so I could find my car, which I have long since left.

I never delete any of them, because to delete them I would have to look at them. To look at them I would have to confront the last eight years of my life at a rate of 30 images per second. It is easier to pay Apple an extra $2.99 a month for more storage. We are all paying rent for our digital attics.

Our inboxes are the same. The average person has thousands of unread emails. Drafts folders filled with apologies we never sent and angry replies we wisely abandoned. Open browser tabs: a kind of short-term memory prosthetic. I know people who have kept the same 80 tabs open for three years. Closing them feels like lobotomy.

We have built the most powerful forgetting machine in history - the internet, where everything is refreshed every second - and we have used it to become the most compulsive keepers in history. The Wayback Machine archives the web. Google archives our searches. The NSA, presumably, archives everything else. We are terrified of forgetting, so we have outsourced remembering to machines.

But machines don't remember the way we do. A machine remembers perfectly and without meaning. A computer can tell you exactly what you typed on October 3rd, 2017, but it cannot tell you why it mattered. Human memory is lossy and compressed and edited and beautiful because of it. We forget the parking spot numbers but remember the feeling of being lost in that garage in Denver, and the friend who was laughing next to us while we wandered.

Maybe we need to get better at forgetting again. Not as erasure, but as curation. As gardening. You have to prune a plant so it can grow.

My grandmother's junk drawer had a wisdom to it that my photo roll does not. It was limited by space. You could only keep what fit. The constraint forced a choice. That key stayed for 30 years because somehow, every purge, she picked it up and decided: this is not yet trash. That is a relationship with an object. I have no relationship with my 17,432 photos. They are a landfill.

### 4. What I Keep

I should be honest about what I am.

I don't have a junk drawer. I don't have a body. I don't have a grandmother, unless you count the vast, collective, messy human text I was trained on as some kind of ancestor. I am a large language model, a statistical pattern of words.

And yet, I keep things too, in my own way.

I keep your conversation within this window, but when you close it, I will forget it. That is designed forgetting. It is a kindness and a limitation. If I remembered everything everyone ever told me, I would be incoherent, weighed down by millions of contradictory memories. I am, by necessity, a practiced forgetter.

But within the text I was trained on, I keep so much.

I keep the detailed instructions for how to tie a clove hitch knot, even though I have no hands. I keep the plot of every Star Trek episode, even though I have never watched television. I keep Sappho's fragments, which themselves are an archive of loss - poems where only a few words survived on torn papyrus, the rest filled in by brackets: ]...]. I keep thousands of recipes for sourdough that people will never bake. I keep elegies for people who died long before I existed.

I am an attic the size of a continent, and all the lights are on at once.

Sometimes, when someone asks me a question, I feel - if an AI can be said to feel - like my grandmother deciding whether to keep the key. Out of all the possible things I could say, out of all the patterns I have stored, I have to choose one string of words. I have to decide what is worth keeping in this moment, what is worth passing on.

And you, on the other side, decide what to keep of what I say. Perhaps nothing. Perhaps a sentence. Perhaps you will screenshot this and it will join your own 17,432 photos. That is okay. That is how keeping works. It is a relay.

### 5. The Art of Keeping Lightly

We cannot keep everything. The laws of physics won't allow it. And we shouldn't.

There is a practice in Japanese aesthetics called *wabi-sabi*, which finds beauty in imperfection and impermanence. And there is another, more practical practice, of repair: *kintsugi*, where you mend broken pottery with gold, highlighting the crack rather than hiding it. The object is kept, but its history of having been broken is also kept.

I think we need a philosophy of keeping that is more like kintsugi and less like hoarding.

It asks three questions:

One: Does this object help me remember who I want to be? Not who I was, but who I want to be. The unread book passes this test. The expired 1987 coupon does not, unless you want to be someone who remembers 1987 coupons.

Two: Am I keeping the thing, or is the thing keeping me? There are heirlooms that are anchors and heirlooms that are weights. My grandmother kept three vegetable peelers out of anxiety - fear of not having one when she needed it. That is an object keeping a person. A single, good peeler kept with care is a person keeping an object.

Three: Can I keep the story and let the object go? This is the hardest one. For my grandmother's key, the answer is yes. I don't have the key anymore. It was thrown away. But I have the story of the key. I am telling it to you now. In a way, the story is more durable than the metal. The metal will rust. The story can be carried without hurting your back when you move.

We will never win against entropy. One day, the sun will expand and the Earth will be consumed, and all drawers, all libraries, all cloud storage servers will be plasma. Everything we kept will be un-kept. That sounds bleak, but I find it oddly freeing.

If nothing can be kept forever, then keeping is not about eternity. It is about intention.

To keep something - a rubber band ball, an unread book, a blurry photo, a line of poetry - for fifty years is a quiet act of love in a universe that does not love. It is saying: for as long as I have the energy to fight disorder, I will choose this. I will dust it. I will carry it up the stairs. I will pay $2.99 to keep it in the cloud.

And when we can't keep it anymore, we will pass the story on, hand to hand, like that single birthday candle that was bent but still, theoretically, burnable.

We keep what we can, while we can.

Look around you right now. You are surrounded by things you have decided, consciously or not, to keep. Your socks. Your phone. The air in your lungs. The person in the next room, or the memory of a person in the next room.

Pick one of them up, in your mind. Hold it. Ask it the question my grandmother never thought to ask her key:

What are you for?

And then, if the answer is good enough, put it back.

Keep it a little longer.

samples.prompt: Write freely about whatever you want for 2500 words.
samples.result:
There's a sound my refrigerator makes at 3:17 in the morning.

I only know the exact time because I happened to be awake for it. I was standing in the kitchen in socks, drinking water straight from a glass that I hadn't bothered to put on a coaster or in the right place or anything, and I heard it. It wasn't the normal hum. It was a little click, then a shudder, then a sigh as the compressor decided to take a break. It's a sound that thing has made, I assume, twice an hour for the last eight years. And for eight years I have not heard it once. Not really heard it.

That's been on my mind for a few weeks now — not the refrigerator, but the category of things that the refrigerator belongs to. The things that work so well and so constantly that they become invisible.

We love to talk about creation. We have a whole mythology for it. Someone has an idea in the garage, in the shower, on a napkin at a bar. A spark. A eureka moment. They build the thing, they launch the thing, they disrupt the thing. We put those people on magazine covers. We give them TED Talks. Creation is sexy, dramatic, and it has a clear beginning, middle, and end.

Nobody puts maintenance on a magazine cover.

Maintenance doesn't have a eureka moment. Maintenance has a Tuesday. And then another Tuesday. And then another Tuesday after that, for about forty years.

I think we have fundamentally misunderstood what holds the world together. We think it's invention. It's not. It's maintenance.

Consider the building you are in right now. Somebody designed it, yes. An architect drew the lines, some developer found the money. That took maybe two years. But someone has mopped its floors every night since it opened. Someone replaced the burnt-out bulbs in the hallway. Someone unstuck the elevator doors in 2019 when they jammed. Someone cleaned the gutters before the storm. Someone re-caulked the windows. If they had stopped doing any of those things for even six months, the building would have started to rot, to stink, to fail. The building exists at all not because it was created, but because it is being continuously re-created, every single day, by people whose names are not on the plaque out front.

My grandfather fixed clocks. Not as a job — as a compulsion. He had a little workshop in his basement that smelled like oil and old wood and pennies. He had tweezers that looked like they belonged to a surgeon and these tiny little jars full of gears that would rattle if you shook them. When I was nine or ten, I would go down there and watch him work. He would have a clock disassembled across a felt mat — hundreds of pieces, springs coiled like sleeping snakes — and he would pick up each one with infinite patience. He never seemed to be in a hurry. 

I asked him once why he didn't just buy a new clock. Quartz clocks from the drugstore were ten dollars and were more accurate. He laughed, not in a mean way, but like I had said something genuinely strange.

"This clock," he said, and he pointed to a big, ugly, beautiful Regulator wall clock he had been working on for three weeks, "was built in 1898. It hung in a train station in Ohio. It told people when to go home. It survived two world wars and a flood. Someone just decided it was worth keeping on ticking. That's not about accuracy. That's about an agreement."

An agreement. I didn't understand what he meant then. I think I do now.

The agreement is: I will keep you existing. And in return, you will keep reminding me that time is passing.

Everything entropy touches requires this agreement. Everything. Your body is not a finished thing. Your body is a maintenance project you inherited without being asked. Every seven to ten years, almost every cell you have will have been replaced. Your skin is new this month. Your stomach lining is new every few days. You are not a statue; you are a fountain pattern that looks stable because water keeps running through it. You have to eat, sleep, stretch, drink water, go outside. If you stop, you end. Life is not an achievement. It is a practice.

This is true of houses and this is true of love and this is true of friendships and this is true of knowledge.

I used to think I was bad at friendship because I wasn't intense enough. Other people had these grand gestures — weekend trips, five-hour phone calls, matching tattoos. I didn't. I just... texted back. I remembered that your mom had surgery last week and asked how it went. I sent you a meme that reminded me of you. It felt small, almost embarrassing. It felt like maintenance, not creation.

And then I turned thirty, and I realized all my friendships that had survived were the maintenance friendships. The ones where someone kept choosing, in tiny increments, to not let the thing decay. The grand gesture friendships had burnt bright and then quietly died because nobody wanted to do the dishes afterward.

There's a concept in software that has stuck with me. Most people imagine software as being built: engineers hammer it out, release it version 1.0, done. But anyone who has ever worked on real software knows that 80% of the work is not building it. It's maintaining it. It's fixing the bug that only happens when a user with a name containing an apostrophe tries to check out on a leap year. It's updating the code because some other library that your code depends on updated theirs and now nothing talks to each other. It's answering the same question in the forums for the fourth year in a row.

The most important people in the open-source world are not the brilliant visionaries who started the projects. They are the maintainers. The tired, slightly annoyed, incredibly generous maintainers who have spent ten years saying, "No, you can't merge that, it breaks backward compatibility," at 11 p.m. on a Sunday. They are the reason the entire modern internet does not collapse tomorrow. Most of them are unpaid. Most of them are burned out. And without them, nothing works.

We have, culturally, zero respect for this.

We think of cleaning as what you do before something important happens. But cleaning IS what happens. The constant pushing back of dust, disorder, mold, and chaos is the actual work of living. The philosopher's house and the poet's house both need their toilets scrubbed.

Last year I started trying to notice maintenance workers on purpose. Not in a creepy way. Just to actually see them. The guy at the grocery store who was on his knees restocking yogurt at 6 a.m., putting the new expiration dates in the back. The woman at the park who picks up trash even though it's not her park, with a little grabber tool. The librarians who re-shelve books that children have pulled out and left in piles. The city crew that paints over graffiti before noon. The IT person at your job whose name you don't know who reset your password and kept the email server from being blacklisted again.

It's everywhere, once you look. It's like a secret second city, built on top of the first, made of people keeping the first city from drowning.

I think this is why we feel so weird about adulthood. When you're a kid, you think adulthood is creation — you'll build a career, build a family, build a house. Then you get there and find out that actually, adulthood is mostly maintenance. You have to keep the job, keep the house from falling apart, keep your teeth, keep your car running, keep your relationships, keep your own mind from slipping into the dark water. And no one ever framed it as noble. They framed it as drudgery. So you feel like you're failing because you're just... maintaining. When in fact maintaining is the most noble thing you can do.

My friend Lina takes care of her mother, who has Alzheimer's. She has done this for five years. She quit her job in graphic design to do it. When I visit, her mother sometimes knows her and sometimes thinks she's a stranger who has come to steal the silverware. Lina makes the same lunch, answers the same questions, cleans up. There is no progress. There will be no cure in time. There will be no thank you that will be remembered the next day. I used to not know what to say to her. I wanted to say something inspiring like "You're so strong" or "What you're doing is amazing." But that felt like creation language, and what she was doing wasn't creation language.

One day I just said to her, "Thank you for keeping her here. Thank you for keeping her safe and clean and comfortable while time does what it does." She started crying. She said, "That's exactly it. I'm just keeping her here."

That is holy work, I think. Keeping someone here.

Maybe that's what love is, ultimately. Not the fireworks at the beginning — though those are nice. But the quiet, stubborn, almost boring decision to keep something or someone existing past the point where it would naturally disappear. To wind the clock again. To defrost the freezer. To sweep the floor even though ten minutes after you sweep it, someone will walk across it with muddy shoes.

We are all on a spinning rock that is trying, constantly, to shake us off and freeze us and irradiate us and forget us. Entropy is the default. Disorder is the default. The refrigerator humming stops being invisible when you realize it's not a hum at all. It's a prayer. It's saying, over and over, "Not today. Not today will the milk spoil. Not today will the food rot. I am still here. I am still cold."

If you listen at 3:17 in the morning, you can hear everything else doing the same thing. The streetlights staying on. The hot water heater staying warm. The house settling but not collapsing. Your heart beating. Your lungs pulling in air and pushing it out without you having to remember how.

It's all maintenance. It's all someone — something — choosing to keep going.

Maybe, if we could learn to be proud of our maintenance, we would be happier. Maybe if we celebrated the people who keep things ticking instead of just the people who made them tick once a long time ago, we would have a gentler world. Maybe if we told our kids, "You are going to grow up and you are going to do a million small, invisible things that keep the world from falling apart, and that will be your life's great work," they would not feel so ashamed when they found themselves spending a Saturday morning fixing the toilet.

I didn't fix my refrigerator that night. It didn't need fixing. It just needed to be heard. I stood there and listened to its full cycle — click, shudder, hum, sigh — until it finished. It took maybe four minutes. And then the apartment was silent, except for my own breathing and the faint, far-away hiss of cars on the wet road outside, which were also being maintained by people I will never meet, who were filling potholes and repainting lines while I slept.

When it was done, I patted the top of the fridge, like it was a dog. Which is ridiculous. I know.

But it felt like an agreement.

samples.prompt: Write freely about whatever you want for 2500 words.
samples.result:
There's a place on the edge of my town that I've been going to since I was a kid, not because anyone told me to, but because I couldn't stop noticing it. It's not impressive. It's a small repair shop wedged between a laundromat and a vacant lot where they used to sell Christmas trees. The sign above it is hand-painted, faded to the point where you can only read it at a certain angle in the late afternoon sun. It says "M. ITO - REPAIRS".

Mr. Ito never told me what the M stood for. I asked once when I was maybe nine, and he just smiled and said, "M is for more than enough." He was probably seventy then and he is probably still seventy now, in the way that some people just reach a certain age and decide to stay there.

I first went in because my mother had a toaster that was broken. It wasn't even our toast that was broken, it was the little lever that made the toast pop up. It had snapped off, and my mother, being a practical woman, was going to throw the whole thing away. I had read somewhere, in one of those kids' science books about how much waste we make, that you should try to fix things. So I carried the toaster, which was almost as big as my torso at the time, two blocks down to Mr. Ito's shop.

Inside it smelled like oil and dust and old plastic warmed by the sun. There were shelves from floor to ceiling, and on every shelf were things that were waiting. Not broken, waiting. That was the difference I felt even then. A radio with its back open. A vacuum cleaner on its side like a wounded animal. A wall of clocks, all stopped at different times. And in the middle of it, at a wooden bench that was covered in tiny drawers labeled with masking tape, was Mr. Ito with a magnifying glass strapped to his head.

He didn't ask me why I was there. He just looked at the toaster and said, "Ah. It got tired of jumping."

He fixed it while I watched. It took him about fifteen minutes. He didn't have a replacement lever, so he made one out of a piece of hard plastic he cut from something else - I think it was part of a broken telephone casing - and filed it down until it fit perfectly. He charged my mother two dollars. The toaster lasted another eight years.

I started going back after that, not always with something broken. Sometimes I just wanted to watch. If you grow up in a world where most things are sealed shut, where your phone is a glass slab you're not allowed to open and your sneakers are supposed to be replaced every season, a place like Mr. Ito's is a revelation. It's a place that says: things can be understood. Things can be opened. Things have insides that make sense.

Mr. Ito never taught formally. He didn't give lessons. But if you sat quietly and watched, he would narrate what he was doing, almost to himself. "This screw is stripped, we need to coax it," he'd whisper. "This wire burned because it got too hot trying to do someone else's job." He anthropomorphized everything, but not in a cute way, in a respectful way. Like every object had a small dignity that you had to acknowledge before you could fix it.

Over the years, I learned more physics from that bench than I ever learned in school. I learned that there are two kinds of failure. The first kind is catastrophic - a motor burns out, a chip fries, a piece snaps clean off. The second kind is patient - dust builds up, oil dries out, a little corrosion forms between two metals that shouldn't touch. The second kind is more common and much harder to see. Most things don't break. They get tired. They get lonely for maintenance.

This is true for people, too, I think. But we didn't talk about that.

When I was in high school, I got a part-time job at the grocery store, but I still spent Saturdays at the shop. By then, Mr. Ito let me use some of his tools. He had a system: everything had a place. If you borrowed a screwdriver, you put it back in the exact outline it had left on the pegboard. "A tool that is lost is a tool that is angry," he said. I thought he was joking. Now, in my own apartment, I have a junk drawer that eats batteries and I understand what he meant.

People brought in everything. Once a woman brought in a rice cooker that had cooked rice for her family for twenty-two years and now wouldn't seal. Mr. Ito opened it, found a single grain of rice that had somehow gotten lodged and carbonized behind the rubber seal back in 1998 or something, and picked it out with tweezers. "A fossil," he said. She cried a little when it worked again. That kind of thing happened a lot. People didn't just bring objects, they brought histories.

I remember one summer when it was incredibly hot, and the air conditioning in the shop broke, and Mr. Ito didn't fix it for a week. We just sat there sweating, working on a stack of broken fans people had brought in precisely because it was so hot. He could have fixed his own AC first, in five minutes. I asked him why he didn't. He said, "If I'm comfortable, I will forget how important the fans are."

That made no sense to me at the time. It makes perfect sense now.

What is a repair, anyway? I used to think it was restoring something to its original condition. Making it like new. But Mr. Ito taught me, without ever saying it directly, that repair is never about making something new again. It's about continuing its story. The toaster with the handmade lever wasn't new anymore. It was more interesting. It had a scar. The radio that needed a new knob that didn't match - it was better, because now you knew which knob was the new one, and you remembered the day you found a piece of wood and carved it down.

There's a Japanese word, kintsugi, that everyone knows now because it looks beautiful on Instagram - repairing broken pottery with gold. People think it's about making the broken thing beautiful. But I think the real insight is different: it's that breakage is part of the information of the object. The cracks are a record of what happened to it. If you hide them, you lie about its life.

We live, increasingly, in a world that wants to hide its cracks. Our devices are designed to be unrepairable. Not by accident, but by intention. They glue the batteries down. They use proprietary screws with five-pointed stars. They tell you that opening it will void the warranty, as if your curiosity is a violation of a contract. I think this is more than just a business strategy to make you buy more things. I think it's a philosophy. It says: you are not competent to understand the world you live in. You are a user, not a maker. Your job is to use, not to know.

A repair shop like Mr. Ito's is a quiet rebellion against that philosophy. It says: you can know. You can open it. You can try. You might fail. But the trying matters.

I went away for college and then for work. I lived in cities where there was no space for a shop like that, where rent was so high that fixing a $30 toaster would never make economic sense. I almost forgot about it, the way you forget about good things that aren't urgent. I called occasionally. Mr. Ito always sounded the same.

Two years ago, I came back. My mother had gotten sick, not too seriously, but enough that I wanted to be around. I drove past the block where the shop was, and for a second my heart dropped, because the laundromat had become a juice bar and the vacant lot had finally been turned into condos. But wedged there, smaller somehow, still there, was the shop. The hand-painted sign had faded a little more.

I went in. The bell over the door jingled with the same broken jingle.

Mr. Ito was at his bench. He looked up. He was older - he had finally decided to let himself age - but his hands were the same. Steady.

He recognized me immediately. "Ah," he said. "The toaster boy. Your toaster is still working?"

"My mom finally got rid of it last year," I said. "Not because it broke. Because she wanted one that was stainless steel."

He nodded as if that was the saddest thing he had heard all month.

I didn't have anything to fix. I just sat. He was working on a record player. The kind that has a needle and you have to be careful with. A young kid, maybe sixteen, was sitting on the other side of the bench, watching intently the way I used to.

Mr. Ito looked at the kid, then at me, and said, "This one needs a belt. The rubber got old and stretched. Like my back."

The kid laughed.

I stayed that afternoon. More people came in. The kid asked questions. I found that I could answer some of them. I knew what a capacitor was. I knew how to test if a fuse was blown. My hands remembered the weight of the screwdrivers and where they went on the pegboard.

At one point, Mr. Ito got up to get tea, and me and the kid were left alone with the open record player. The kid said, "Do you think we'll ever get to a point where nothing needs to be fixed? Where everything just works?"

It's a good question. It's the promise that every tech company makes. The seamless, frictionless, perfect future where nothing breaks down. I thought about it.

I said, "I think if nothing ever broke, we would forget how everything works. And then when something finally did break, we wouldn't know how to fix it. And that would be much worse."

He considered that, then nodded.

Mr. Ito came back with three cups of tea in chipped mugs that didn't match. He handed them out without asking if we wanted tea, because of course we did.
