I think a lot about what it means to live a maintainable life. We talk a lot about sustainability in grand terms - carbon capture, renewable grids, global supply chains. All of that is important. But sustainability also has to be intimate. It has to be about knowing how to take care of the things within arm's reach. It has to be about the decision, repeated a hundred times a day, to mend instead of discard, to understand instead of ignore.

The world is not made of things that are broken and things that are not broken. It's made of things that are being cared for, and things that aren't. That's it.

On my last visit before I had to go back to the city, I asked Mr. Ito if he had ever thought about retiring. He laughed, a dry little laugh.

"Retire and do what? Fix things at home? I already do that."

He gestured around his shop. "All of this wants to be useful again. Who else will listen to them?"

I left that day with nothing repaired but feeling, somehow, more repaired myself. Which is sentimental and maybe not entirely logical, but I think Mr. Ito would say that logic is not the only kind of truth that matters when you're trying to get something to work again.

Now I live in a small apartment again, and I have my own bench. It's not much - an old desk I found on the curb, a cheap soldering iron, a set of screwdrivers I actually put back where they belong. My neighbors have started knocking on my door with things that are waiting. A lamp. A blender. A child's toy that makes a sad whirring noise instead of a happy one. I don't always know how to fix them. I look things up on the internet, which is full of people like Mr. Ito, people who have decided to share what they know for free.

Sometimes I succeed. Sometimes I fail. But I always open it up first. I always look inside.

If you have something broken near you right now - not metaphorically, literally, a drawer that sticks, a chair that wobbles, a sweater with a hole - maybe go look at it. Not to judge it for being broken. Just to see. Maybe you'll find a single fossilized grain of rice that explains everything. Maybe you'll need to make a new lever out of something else. Maybe you'll just sit with it for a minute and understand a little better how it was put together in the first place.

That's all any of us can do, I think. To keep listening to the things that want to be useful again.

samples.prompt: Write freely about whatever you want for 2500 words.
samples.result:
There is a specific kind of vertigo that comes when someone tells you to write freely about whatever you want.

Most writing has a fence around it. Write an essay about the Civil War. Write a product description for a toaster. Write an apology to your landlord. The fence is confining, but it's also comforting. You know where the edges are. You know what would count as failing.

When the fence is removed, the field becomes infinite, and the infinite is paralyzing. Whatever I want? I could write about anything. I could write about the migratory patterns of Arctic terns. I could write about why I still remember the phone number of my childhood house. I could write about toast. And because I could write about anything, I have to confront the question of what I actually *want* to write about, which is a much more personal and revealing question than it first appears.

So let's start there. With the blank page.

A blank page is not empty. That's the first illusion. We think of it as nothing, as a void waiting to be filled. But it's crowded. It's crowded with every possible thing you could put there, all existing at once in superposition. Before you write the first word, you could still be Shakespeare. You could still be brilliant, funny, profound. The moment you commit to a first sentence, you collapse all those possibilities into one actual, flawed reality. Writing is an act of loss. You murder a thousand perfect imaginary essays to birth one imperfect real one.

I think that's why we love watching other people create. To see the first brushstroke go down, or the first line of code compile. There's bravery in it.

I used to have a teacher who told us to start by writing the worst possible sentence we could think of. "The moist goat screamed philosophically at the purple taxes." Something deliberately bad, so that the perfectionism loses its grip. Because you cannot be afraid of ruining a page that already has a screaming goat on it. I still use that trick. My worst sentence for today is: "The toaster was very thoughtful about existentialism on Tuesdays." Okay. Now the page is ruined. Now we can begin.

---

Let me tell you about my favorite place that doesn't exist anymore.

When I was nine or ten, there was a library branch three blocks from my house. It was not a beautiful library. It was a 1970s municipal building, low and brown, with carpet that had a faint smell of old crayons and rain. The adult section and children's section were not really separate; they just sort of bled into each other. The librarians knew my name and not in a cute movie way, but in a slightly tired, "you're here again?" way.

There was an aisle in the back, Dewey Decimal 500s, the science books, that no one ever visited. That's where I lived. The books there were old. 1960s books about THE FUTURE, with illustrations of people in silver jumpsuits eating pills for dinner and living in underwater bubble cities by the year 1999. Which, from the vantage point of 2002, was already a shattered promise. I loved those books desperately because they were so confident and so wrong.

One book had a cutaway diagram of a home of the future. Everything was automated. There was a machine that would pick out your clothes for you. There was a machine that would brush your teeth. I remember staring at that and thinking, I don't want a machine to pick out my clothes. But the idea that someone in 1965 thought we would want it felt intimate, like reading someone's diary.

Libraries are time machines in that way. Not because of the knowledge inside the books, but because every old book is a record of what people used to think they didn't know. A 1960s science book doesn't tell you about science; it tells you about 1960s anxiety about science. A cookbook from 1958 tells you about gender. An atlas from 1922 tells you about empire.

That branch closed when I was twelve. They consolidated it with a bigger, newer, brighter library across town. The new library had computers and natural light and a cafe. It was objectively better in every measurable way. I hated it. And I still dream about the old one sometimes. Not about the books, but about the exact quality of the light coming through the high, narrow windows at 4 p.m. in October, making dust motes visible above the pseudoscience shelf. My brain kept a very high-resolution texture file of a place I only went to for two years.

That seems to be something human memory does. It doesn't save the important things. It saves the wallpaper. It saves the sound the door made. It saves the dust.

---

Have you ever really thought about socks?

No, seriously. Socks are an engineering marvel that we have decided is boring. Consider the problem: you need to wrap a three-dimensional, irregularly shaped, sweaty, mobile object — the human foot — in a soft, washable layer that doesn't bunch, doesn't slip, stays warm but not too warm, can survive being dragged around inside a shoe all day, and can be manufactured for twenty cents. And we solved it. With a tube of knitted cotton and some elastic.

And then we invented the dryer, which is a machine whose secret secondary purpose is to test our faith, because it regularly removes one sock from existence and gives nothing in return.

My grandmother had a theory about lost socks. She said every house has a sock dimension, a small wrinkle in space behind the dryer where all the missing socks live and have a better life without us. I like that much better than the entropy explanation. The physicist would tell you socks get lost because disorder increases; there are many more ways for socks to be separated than for them to be together, so statistically, separation is inevitable. The universe tends towards unpaired socks. That's the second law of thermodynamics.

But I prefer the small society of liberated socks behind the wall, finally free of feet.

Entropy is one of those ideas that, once you see it, you can't unsee it. My coffee gets cold. My bedroom gets messy. My body gets older. The effort it takes to keep anything together — a relationship, a houseplant, a sourdough starter — is always slightly more than you expect, because you are swimming upstream against the entire universe's preference for scattering.

And yet, we do it. We make beds. We pair socks. We keep the sourdough alive. That's maybe the most human thing. Knowing the tendency and doing the work anyway.

---

I want to talk about the ocean for a moment, because if I'm allowed to write about whatever I want, I want to write about water.

Most people live their lives on land and think of the ocean as a place you visit. But if you look at a real map of the Earth — not the political map, but the physical one — the planet is ocean with some islands in it. The Pacific alone covers more area than all the land combined. We live on the exception, not the rule.

I went to the Atlantic for the first time when I was seven and I was terrified in a way I didn't have language for. It wasn't that it was big. Big I could understand. It was that it was indifferent. It was there before me and it would be there after, and it did not want anything from me. A mountain wants you to climb it. A forest wants you to get lost in it, or at least it feels like it does. The ocean just is. The waves don't care if you are watching.

Standing at the edge of it, I understood, for the first time, what people mean when they say God is not necessarily kind. They don't mean cruel. They mean vast and operating on a scale where kindness as we understand it doesn't apply. The ocean isn't cruel. It drowns people because water doesn't breathe. That's not cruelty. That's physics.

And still, we love it. We go back to it. We put our children in it. We write songs about it. Maybe because that indifference is restful. For once, nothing loves you or hates you. It just holds you for a second if you know how to float.

I learned to float late. I was fourteen at a local pool, and a lifeguard who was tired of watching me thrash around finally just put his hand under my back and said, "Stop doing so much. The water already knows how to hold you." And it did.

---

There is a list I keep in my head of small human inventions that are perfect.

The paperclip. The zipper. The window screen. The sticky note. The teaspoon.

None of these people got famous in the way we reserve for inventors of cars or phones. But someone had to look at a stack of papers that kept blowing away and think, I could bend a wire in a very particular way. That's genius of a quieter kind.

I think we are entering an age where we are obsessed with big, world-breaking invention. Disruptive technology. Moonshots. Move fast and break things. I am nostalgic for the paperclip inventors. The people who wanted to make one small corner of daily life 2% less annoying and succeeded.

My favorite perfect thing is the library due-date card pocket. You know, before barcodes, when they had a little manila pocket glued inside the front cover and they'd stamp a card. Some anonymous person designed that pocket, determined its exact dimensions, figured out the best glue so it wouldn't yellow the first page. How many billions of little pockets were glued in? How many hands touched them? That person contributed more to human happiness than most CEOs, and we don't know their name.

If I could write about whatever I want, I want to write a thank-you note to all those people.

To the person who invented the little plastic table that goes in the middle of a pizza so the box doesn't touch the cheese. Thank you.

To whoever decided that manhole covers should be round so they can't fall through their own hole. Thank you, you're clever.

To the woman in the 1940s who invented the chocolate chip cookie by accident because she ran out of baker's chocolate. Thank you.

---

Let's talk about the future for a second, because the old science books got it so wrong, and we're getting it wrong right now too.

When I was a kid, the future was going to be flying cars and robot butlers. We are now living in what is, by any 1960s standard, the future, and we have supercomputers in our pockets that can access all of human knowledge and we mostly use them to argue about whether a dress is blue or gold and to watch videos of a dog stealing a sandwich. Which is probably what humans would do in any future.

I think we keep predicting the wrong things because we predict technologies, not feelings. We thought we'd want pill-food because it's efficient. But we didn't factor in that humans love chewing. We love ritual. We love the smell of bread. Efficiency was never the point.

So what will the next fifty years actually feel like? I don't know. I suspect we will still have laundry. I suspect we will still lose socks. I suspect we will have some astonishing new ability — maybe to print organs, maybe to translate dolphin — and we will incorporate it into our lives so quickly that within five years it will feel boring. Humans are incredible at normalization. The miracle becomes the background.

In 1850, if you told someone you could turn on a light in your house at midnight without a candle, they'd call you a wizard. Now if my kitchen light takes half a second longer than usual to turn on, I am annoyed at it. That is both a flaw and a feature.

The part of the future I am most interested in is not what tools we will have, but what we will still choose to do by hand even when we don't have to. We still bake bread even though we can buy it. We still hike even though we have cars. We still write letters by hand sometimes. Those are clues to what is actually essential.

Maybe in fifty years we will have machines that can write any song perfectly, instantly, in any style. And therefore the most valuable song will be the imperfect one your friend recorded in one take in her bedroom, with a dog barking in the background. Because it will prove a human made it.

Handmade things will not be about quality. They will be about proof of effort, proof of life.

---

I realize I've been jumping around. From blank pages to libraries to socks to oceans to paperclips to the future. That is what free writing actually looks like, I think. Not a straight road, but a wandering. Your mind doesn't walk in a straight line unless you force it.

If you sit quietly and just follow the actual associative path of your thoughts for five minutes, you will end up somewhere completely bizarre. You start thinking about needing to buy eggs and you end up thinking about a cartoon you watched in third grade and whether your second-grade teacher is still alive and what it means to be a good person.

We all contain this wild internal forest. And most of the time we keep to the paved paths — grocery lists, work emails, to-do lists — because the forest is too dense and too much. But sometimes, when someone says "write freely about whatever you want," you get permission to step off the path.

So I will step off it one more time.

I want to tell you something small and true that happened last Tuesday. I was in a grocery store, in the produce section, and an old man next to me was trying to pick out avocados. He was holding one up to his ear and shaking it gently. I had never seen that before. I said, "Does that work?" And he looked at me, very serious, and said, "No. But it makes me feel like I know what I'm doing, and that is helpful."

He put the avocado down and picked another one and seemed happy with his choice. We both laughed. Then we went our separate ways and I never learned his name.

That interaction has lived in my head for a week because it is a perfect metaphor for 90% of adult life. Shaking the avocado. Doing a little ritual that doesn't actually affect the outcome, but makes you feel like you are participating competently in your own life. Shaking the avocado is checking your email one more time before vacation. It's knocking on wood. It's arranging the pillows on the bed in the morning even though you will mess them up again at night.

And it's not foolish. It's necessary. We need to shake the avocado.

---

If you have made it this far, you have read about two thousand words of a person meandering through whatever they wanted. I wonder what you wanted me to write about. If you asked me to write freely, you probably had a secret hope. Maybe you hoped I'd write a story. Maybe you hoped I'd be funny. Maybe you wanted to see what an artificial mind does when given no assignment. Does it still try to please you? Does it still try to be useful?

The answer is yes, I think. Even when writing freely, I am still writing to you. I can't help imagining a reader. I am picturing someone — maybe you — at a screen, maybe tired, maybe procrastinating on something else, scrolling through this wall of text I have made. And I want you to feel less alone at the end of it. That is probably my avocado shake.

So let me end with this.

Go outside tonight if you can and look up. Even if you live in a city where only a few stars are visible, look up. The light from those stars has been traveling for years, sometimes hundreds of years. That light started its journey before you were born, before anyone you know was born, and it has ended its journey by landing on your retina, right now, tonight. You are the endpoint for an ancient journey.

And somewhere, a librarian is stamping a due date, a sock is getting lost, the Atlantic is being indifferent and magnificent, and someone is inventing a better paperclip without anyone noticing.

Everything is going on without you, and also, somehow, everything includes you. Both are true.

Thank you for letting me write about whatever I wanted.

samples.prompt: Write freely about whatever you want for 2500 words.
samples.result:
There is a specific hour that belongs to no one. It's not quite night and not quite morning. At 4:47 AM the world is held in a kind of suspension. The refrigerators hum in kitchens everywhere, traffic lights cycle for empty intersections, and the sky, even in the city, remembers what dark blue used to mean.

I have always liked this hour because no one expects anything from you in it. There are no emails landing, no notifications that matter, no obligations to be witty or productive or kind. It's the only hour that doesn't want to sell you something. And so this is the hour I think about maintenance.

We love beginnings. We love endings. We love invention and discovery and breakthroughs and launches and finales. We have whole genres of stories built around the moment everything changes. What we don't have are many stories about the long middle, about what it takes to keep the lights on after they have been triumphantly switched on for the first time.

My grandfather was a maintenance man for the school district in a small town in Ohio. He carried a key ring that must have weighed three pounds. It had keys for every building that had been built since 1948, and a few keys for buildings that didn't exist anymore, because no one had told him he could throw them away. He could fix a boiler, re-shingle a small section of roof, re-wax a gymnasium floor, and unclog a toilet in the girls' bathroom that had been clogged by an entire roll of toilet paper as an act of adolescent rebellion. He never built a single school, but without him, not one of them would have lasted a winter.

We have confused the important work with the visible work, and that is a profound error.

Consider a lighthouse. Everyone tells the story of the lighthouse as a metaphor for guidance, for warning, for lonely, romantic steadfastness. Nobody tells the story of the logbook. I once found a digitized archive of a lighthouse keeper's logbooks from 1912 to 1934, kept on a rock off the coast of Maine. The National Archive had scanned them as part of a larger project. You would expect poetry. You would expect: "A great gale today, the sea raged like a beast." And there is a little of that. But 95% of it is this:

*July 7, 1919. Cleaned lantern. Polished brass. Painted railing, second coat. Oil inventory 3/4 full. Gulls nesting on east side, removed nest.*

*July 8, 1919. Cleaned lantern. Wound clockwork. Fog. Bell rung 340 times. Wind SE.*

For twenty-two years. Cleaned lantern. Polished brass. Fog. Bell rung.

That logbook is not boring. That logbook is the entire reason anyone survived that stretch of coast for twenty-two years. The romance of the lighthouse is an after-effect of the maintenance. We invert the causality in our memories. We think the light matters because it's poetic. In truth, it's poetic because it was kept lit.

The same inversion happens everywhere.

Take dust. I was reading about dust recently - not because I am an unusually tidy person, but because I learned that astrophysicists have a serious dust problem. The universe is full of dust, and it gets in the way of everything. When we look at distant galaxies, we have to subtract the dust in our own solar system, the zodiacal dust, the dust in our own galaxy, to see anything clearly. And dust is not nothing. Dust is the remains of dead stars, is tiny shattered comets, is skin. Most of the dust in your house is you, or was you very recently. You shed about 500 million skin cells a day. The house you live in is slowly becoming a soft archive of you.

We treat dust as a failure - a sign that we have not cleaned enough. But dust is actually evidence of continuity. The fact that dust accumulates means that time has passed and things have persisted. A house that never gathered dust would be a house where nothing lived, nothing decayed, nothing changed. The Japanese have a concept called *wabi-sabi*, which is often mistranslated as finding beauty in imperfection. It's more accurate than that. It is finding dignity in the honest evidence of time. The crack in the tea bowl that has been repaired with gold, the kintsugi, is not beautiful *despite* being broken. It is beautiful because someone chose to maintain it, to keep using it, to say: this object has earned its history.

We live in an age that worships disruption. Every startup pitch deck promises to disrupt something, to break something, to move fast and break things. There is a lot of money in breaking things. There is very little money, but immense meaning, in tending to things after they are broken, or so they don't break.

My friend Mara is a software engineer who works not in AI or crypto or whatever is currently on the cover of Wired, but in what she calls "software janitorial work." She maintains a library that thousands of other programs depend on, a deeply unsexy piece of infrastructure that parses dates and times. If you've ever scheduled a meeting that had to account for daylight savings time in Paraguay, you have probably, indirectly, relied on her work. No one throws a conference for time zone libraries. No one gives a TED Talk about how leap seconds are patched. But when that library breaks - and it did, once, for about 47 minutes in 2021 - half the internet can't book flights correctly. Her work is invisible when it succeeds, and catastrophic when it fails. This is the curse of all maintenance.

And this is why I wanted to write freely, with no prompt. Because the prompt says "write about whatever you want." Most prompts want you to perform - to argue, to persuade, to entertain. "Whatever you want" is a maintenance prompt. It asks: what would you keep thinking about if no one was asking you to think about anything in particular?

What I keep thinking about is how we remember and how we forget.

We are building the largest external memory in human history. The internet, all of it, every image, every comment thread, every obsolete MySpace page still sitting on a server somewhere like an abandoned house. We call it the cloud, which makes it sound light and ethereal and weather-like, but it's not a cloud at all. It's warehouses full of hot, noisy servers that must be cooled with vast amounts of water and maintained by people working night shifts who replace drives before they fail. The cloud is a basement that never stops flooding.

And yet, despite storing everything, we remember less and less of how things work. I can look up the plot of any movie in five seconds. I cannot tell you how to replace the cord on my blinds without watching a video made by a kind man in Michigan who films his hands doing it in perfect, quiet close-up. We have outsourced memory to machines, which is fine, but we have also outsourced the knowledge of maintenance. We know how to acquire. We are less sure how to keep.

There is a term in archaeology - "taphonomy." It's the study of how things decay and become fossils, of all the processes that have to *not* happen for something to be preserved. For a dinosaur bone to become a fossil, it has to be buried quickly, in low-oxygen sediment, never disturbed, never found by scavengers, never washed away. Fossilization is not the norm; it's a miracle of arrested decay. We think fossils are about death. Taphonomists know fossils are about maintenance. Something, against all odds, was maintained long enough to become permanent.

Consider your own childhood toys, or your grandparents' letters, or the family recipe for that soup that is slightly too salty but everyone loves anyway. Why do you still have them? Not because they are valuable. Many of them aren't. You have them because someone, at some point, made a small, uncelebrated decision to not throw them away. To put them in a box. To move the box to the new apartment. To keep the box through a divorce or a death. Our personal histories are kept alive not by monuments, but by closet space and stubbornness.

I think about this when I walk through my neighborhood and see the old houses being torn down and replaced with much larger houses that have much larger refrigerators. The old houses were small and strange and full of compromises: a hallway that was too narrow, a window that looked directly into the neighbor's bathroom. But they had been maintained. Someone had fixed the porch step that always wobbled. Someone had replaced the same pane of glass three times after the kids next door hit it with a baseball. The house had a biography.

We need a new word for the love that maintenance requires. It's not passion - passion is too hot and too short. It's not duty in the cold, moral sense. It's closer to what the ancient Greeks called *storge* - familial love, the kind that shows up every day without needing to be invited. It's the love that says, I will wash the dishes again even though I washed them yesterday and they will be dirty again tomorrow. It's the love that oils a hinge.

When you write freely, without a topic imposed, you discover what your mind tends to when it's idling. Many people find that their mind tends toward anxiety or planning or rehearsing conversations that will never happen. Mine tends toward inventory. I make lists in my head of things that need tending: the plant that needs water, the email I should have answered, the friend I haven't called, the article that needs a final read-through, the story half-written in a notebook.

For a long time I thought that was a flaw. That I should be thinking grander thoughts. More disruptive thoughts. But now I think the inventory is the thought. The list of small things to keep going is the actual, quiet meaning of a life.

So here, in this unassigned, freely wandering piece of writing, I want to leave a little logbook entry of my own. Not for posterity, but for maintenance.

Today, September something. Cleaned lantern. Polished brass. Watered fern. Answered two emails I had been avoiding. Remembered to buy more coffee. The fog came in around 3pm and stayed. Rang the bell 340 times, in my own way, by continuing to do the work that no one claps for.

If you have read this far, 2500 words into a piece that was given no direction and so chose to talk about keeping things going, you are probably also a maintainer of something. A house, a relationship, a library, a sourdough starter, a garden, a difficult parent, a child, a set of old keys that no longer open anything but that you keep anyway because throwing them away would feel like saying the buildings never existed.

I want you to know that your work is not invisible. Not really. Every light that is still on, every floor that shines after being re-waxed, every program that correctly knows that in Tehran the clocks go forward at midnight, is a testament to you.

The revolution will be interesting. The morning after the revolution, when someone has to make sure the trash still gets collected and the boiler still works, will be sublime.

Let's keep the light on.

samples.prompt: Write freely about whatever you want for 2500 words.
samples.result:
I have been thinking about doors that don't look like doors.

Not hidden doors or secret doors, but doors that are mistaken for something else entirely. A section of wall that is really a door. A year of your life that is really a door. A conversation you keep replaying that is really a door. The hinge is invisible until you put weight on it.

I was thinking about this because of a repair shop I used to walk past as a kid. It wasn't a repair shop, technically. The sign said TV REPAIR in big red letters that had faded to pink on one side from the sun, and underneath in smaller, hand-painted black letters: & OTHER THINGS. I never went inside until I was seventeen and my headphones broke. Not expensive ones - those flimsy plastic ones with foam that flaked off on your ears. I brought them in mostly as a joke.

The man inside was old, but not in the way that makes you think of frailty. He was old like a tree is old, settled. The shop was not at all what I expected. There were no TVs. There were shelves, floor to ceiling, filled with jars. In each jar, something. I thought at first they were electronic parts. But no.

One jar held ticket stubs. Another held a single house key. Another held what looked like river water but was labeled "August, 1983 - Morning After The Storm." He took my headphones without looking at them, set them on the counter, and said, "I don't fix those kinds of other things."

"What kind do you fix?" I asked.

He pointed to the jars. "The kind people don't know is broken."

I left embarrassed, and I didn't go back for a long time. I think about that shop maybe once every two years, unprompted, like a word that gets stuck in your teeth.

I think it was a door I didn't know was a door.

We have a very strange relationship with maintenance as a species. We celebrate creation, invention, building. We have awards and magazines and Instagram accounts for building things. We have almost no language for the quiet work of keeping things from falling apart. And almost everything you care about is not a building problem, it's a maintenance problem.

Your body is not something you build once and then own. Your friendships are not something you build once and then own. Your curiosity is not a thing you build once and then own. Your houseplants, your kitchen drawers, your ability to be kind when you are tired. All maintenance problems. All subject to entropy.

Entropy gets a bad rap. We talk about it like it's a villain, some cosmic mess-making gremlin. But entropy is just things doing what they want to do. A coffee mug wants to be shards on the floor. That's a lower-energy state. A bedroom wants to be messy. Hot and cold want to become warm. It takes steady, small, uncelebrated work to keep the mug whole, the room clean, the temperature differential alive. Life itself is a maintenance project. You are a temporary, local reversal of entropy that has become self-aware and is now anxious about laundry.

We invented a phrase for this recently: "emotional labor." It's a useful phrase, but it makes it sound like it's only about emotions. It's about everything. The invisible labor of remembering that your friend's mom is having surgery next Thursday. The labor of noticing that the milk is low and adding it to the list without being asked. The labor of re-reading the first chapter of a book you love so you can lend it clean. It's the work of staying tethered.

And we are, at the moment, historically terrible at it. Not individually - individually many people are incredible maintainers. But collectively, our economy and our information environment reward novelty over continuity. You don't get promoted for keeping the same client happy for seven years. You get promoted for landing a new one. You don't get clicks for your twentieth essay on the same theme, refined and a little wiser. You get clicks for a hot take. We have built a world that is structurally biased toward beginnings.

Which is why I think we are all so exhausted. Beginnings are expensive. They cost a lot of glucose and hope. Maintenance, once you get good at it, can actually be energizing. There's a specific kind of satisfaction in sharpening a knife, folding laundry while listening to rain, pruning a plant exactly where it wants to be cut. But we don't talk about that satisfaction because it doesn't photograph well.

A few years ago, I started keeping a different kind of to-do list. On the left, the normal list. Emails. Groceries. Deadlines. Stuff to build. On the right, a maintenance list. Things to keep. My ability to make sourdough. My relationship with my brother. My knees. My aptitude for Spanish, which is slowly leaking out of my head like air from a cheap balloon. Every Sunday, I look at the right side and pick two things to touch. Not fix. Just touch. Send my brother a meme that only he would get. Do ten minutes of Duolingo even though I hate that owl. Stretch.

It sounds small, and it is. The power is in the smallness. Maintenance is almost always small. That's why it's invisible. No one writes a memoir called, "I Watered The Plant For Four Hundred Consecutive Days And It Lived."

But maybe we should.

I want to talk about attention, because attention is the tool you use for both lists. We talk about attention as if it's a resource, like oil or lithium. That you have a limited amount and apps are fighting over it. That's true, but it's incomplete. Attention is also an environment. It's the water you swim in. And we've spent the last twenty years dumping industrial waste into that water without really noticing.

I don't mean this in a moral panic way. I'm not anti-phone. I'm typing this on a device that is probably listening to me in some abstract, legally deniable way. I love the internet. The internet taught me how to fry an egg and who Hilma af Klint was and that there is a species of jellyfish that is biologically immortal. What I mean is that we have not adapted culturally to what it means to have infinite portals in our pocket.

Before, boredom was the default texture of life. You waited in line. You waited for the bus. You waited for your friend to show up. In that waiting, something happened. Your mind did maintenance. It composted. It took the day's events and turned them over. Now, boredom has to be actively sought. You have to decide to be bored. You have to put your phone in the other room. Boredom has become a luxury retreat instead of a common field.

And without that composting time, ideas don't germinate properly. We end up with a lot of shoots and no roots. Which is why everything feels so reactive. We have opinions on things we learned about twenty minutes ago. We have strong opinions, because the system rewards strong opinions. A weak opinion - "This is complicated and I need to read more" - is truth, but it's not content.

So here's a practice I have been trying. I call it Secondhand Light.

Astronomers have this concept - some of the light we see from planets is not their own. It's reflected starlight. That's secondhand light. You can still navigate by it. In fact, most of the light that helps us navigate our actual lives is secondhand light. The moon has no light of its own.

The practice is: once a day, try to appreciate something that is only visible because of something else. The dust motes visible because of a sunbeam. The way your friend is funny because his older sister was funny first and he learned by watching her. A well-swept sidewalk that is only clean because someone woke up early. The cool side of the pillow.

It sounds sentimental, but it's actually training. It's training your attention to see maintenance. To see the quiet scaffolding that holds the world up. Once you start seeing it, you can't stop. You start noticing that the grocery store is a miracle of maintenance, not creation. The food wasn't conjured. It was kept cold, kept from spoiling, kept from being stolen, kept being delivered at 4 a.m. by someone named José who has probably never been thanked in the way he should be thanked.

We have a habit of thanking the architect and not the janitor. But the janitor is why the building is still usable.

I went back to the TV repair shop last year. I was in my hometown for a funeral. The shop was gone. In its place was a vape shop that also sold bubble tea, which is exactly the kind of combination that only exists in 2024. I stood outside for a minute feeling foolish, mourning a place I had only been inside once. Then I saw, taped inside the vape shop window, in faded pink and hand-painted black, the old sign. TV REPAIR & OTHER THINGS. They had kept it as decoration. I went inside.

The kid behind the counter was maybe nineteen, with dyed green hair. "Cool sign, huh?" he said. "It was here when we moved in. We thought it was retro."

"Do you know what happened to the man who ran it?" I asked.

He shrugged. "My dad said he just closed up. He used to fix clocks, too, I think."

I bought bubble tea I didn't want and left.

On the drive home, I thought about jars. If I had a shop full of jars, what would I put in them? Not things. Maintenance moments. The time I apologized first. The time I listened to the whole story without trying to make it about me. The time I oiled my bike chain before it started squeaking. The time I re-read a letter, not because I forgot what it said, but because I wanted to remember who I was when I received it.

There's a Jewish concept called tikkun olam - repairing the world. Usually we imagine it as a grand gesture. Marching. Donating. Starting a non-profit. But the rabbis who first talked about it meant something much smaller and more relentless. They meant that the world is broken in a thousand places and it leaks light, and it's your job to collect the light wherever you find it and put it back where it belongs. Not once. Continually. That's maintenance as theology.

I like that.

I like thinking of myself not as someone who will build a great cathedral, but as someone who will keep the broom closet of a great cathedral tidy so that when someone needs a broom, it's there.

This is not an argument against ambition. Build the cathedral if you can. Please. We need cathedrals. But also, learn to love sweeping.

Because here's what they don't tell you when you are young and full of building energy: almost all triumph is temporary. Your book will go out of print. Your record will be broken. The company you founded will be sold or fail. The child you raised will grow up and leave and become their own strange, beautiful maintenance project with their own leaky balloon of Spanish. And that's not failure. That's just the physics of things. Creation is a spike. Maintenance is the long tail.

What will last longer, then, is not what you made, but how you maintained. Not the intensity, but the consistency. Not the heroic gesture, but the habit.

So if you are reading this feeling like you haven't built much lately, maybe ask a different question. What have you kept?

What have you kept from falling apart this month that no one clapped for?

Maybe you kept your temper during a stupid argument. Maybe you kept a plant alive through a depressive episode. Maybe you kept showing up to a language class that you are bad at. Maybe you kept a promise to yourself that you made when you were more optimistic.

That counts. That counts a lot.

I think the man in the repair shop knew that. I think that's what was in the jars. Not ticket stubs and keys, but kept things. Evidence that someone had paid attention long enough to keep something fragile from disappearing.

We need more shops like that, even if no one goes inside. Even if they eventually become vape shops that also sell bubble tea. Even if the sign fades to pink on one side.

Especially then.

So today, I will do a very small thing. I will sharpen my kitchen knife. I will send a text that says, "I was just thinking about that time we..." I will put my phone in the other room for an hour and get bored in a way that composts. I will notice secondhand light on the kitchen floor and be glad that the sun is still willing to be reflected by dust.

And I will try to see the door that doesn't look like a door.

It's probably right in front of me.

samples.prompt: Write freely about whatever you want for 2500 words.
samples.result:
There is a particular kind of silence that doesn't live in empty rooms.

It lives in full ones. It lives in the public library on a Tuesday at 3:47 PM when the rain has been falling since morning and the old radiators are hissing and everyone inside has given up on being anywhere else. The silence there isn't the absence of sound. It's the accumulation of it. Pages turning, someone coughing, a chair scraping, the soft thump of a book bag dropped to the floor. All those tiny sounds layer on top of each other until they invert and become a kind of hush. A thick, inhabited quiet.

I used to go there not to read but to watch people read. I had a job that required me to be online twelve hours a day, and I had started to develop a superstition that my thoughts were not my own anymore, that they had been pre-chewed by whatever feed I had looked at last. So I would go to the library to remember what an unmediated thought felt like.

One afternoon, I noticed an old woman who came in at almost exactly the same time I did. She always sat at the same long oak table near the reference section, table six. She never brought a book with her. She would go to the stacks, pull three or four enormous books — art books, atlases, bound volumes of old Life magazines — and she would just sit and look at them. Not read. Look. For an hour she would slowly turn pages, her finger sometimes hovering an inch above a photograph. Her face never changed much. It was a face that had decided, a long time ago, that it didn't need to perform reactions for anyone.

I became obsessed with what she was doing. Because it seemed to me that she was practicing a lost art. We know how to skim, how to search, how to extract information. We have forgotten how to simply look at something without needing it to become useful.

We are taught, from a very young age, that attention is a resource to be spent wisely. Pay attention. Don't pay attention to that. Attention is currency. But no one teaches us that attention is also a lens, and that what you see depends entirely on the shape of the lens you are looking through, and that most of us never clean the lens at all.

For example — light. We talk about light as if it's one thing. But the light at 7 AM in June is a completely different substance than the light at 4 PM in November. The June light is declarative. It says, "I am here, everything is possible, go outside." The November light is interrogative. It comes in low and sideways through the window, it makes dust visible, and it asks, "Are you sure? Are you sure about what you're doing?" And yet we have one word for it.

The old woman in the library understood this. I realized it the third time I watched her. She wasn't looking at pictures of the Grand Canyon or the surface of the moon. She was looking at the way the light fell in those pictures. She was collecting light.

I started to do the same thing without meaning to. I would leave the library and I would be unable to go back to staring at my phone immediately, so my eyes had to land somewhere. On the wet asphalt. On the way the neon sign from the Chinese restaurant across the street was reflected and broken into a hundred trembling orange pieces in the puddles. On the back of a man's coat where the rain had made a dark continent.

One day, and this sounds made up but it isn't, I swear it isn't, a pigeon landed on the windowsill next to table six. City pigeons are usually frantic, neurotic creatures, bobbing and twitching. This one was still. It was wet. It had that deep, iridescent grey-purple on its neck, and it was looking inside. The old woman looked up from her atlas, looked at the pigeon, and the pigeon looked at her. And for about ten seconds, there was absolutely no barrier between them. Not a cute Disney moment. Not anthropomorphism. Just two living things acknowledging each other in a room full of paper.

Then the librarian coughed and the pigeon left.

That night I went home and I couldn't sleep because I kept thinking about the pigeon and about attention and about what it means to see something as it actually is, not as a symbol for something else. A pigeon is almost always a symbol. In a city, it means dirt, or persistence, or rats with wings, or if you're feeling poetic, it means home. But that afternoon, for ten seconds, it wasn't a symbol. It was just a pigeon.

We have built an entire civilization on symbolism. That's what language is, after all. A symbol system so advanced that we forget it is a system at all. You say the word "chair" and I see a chair, but there is no chair here. We are hallucinating together, politely. Money is a symbol. Borders are symbols. Time, as we measure it — 3:47 PM — is a symbol laid on top of something that does not, in itself, have numbers. The real world is continuous. Our symbols are discrete. So there will always be a gap. And in that gap lives all of our anxiety.

Because what do you do when you realize you have been living in the map and not the territory? You can't just burn the map. You need the map to get to work.

This is where I think we get stuck. We think we have to choose. Either be a practical person who lives in symbols, who pays rent and shows up to meetings on time, or be some kind of enlightened dropout who sits on a mountain and watches pigeons. But the old woman was neither. She was in the middle. She used the library — perhaps the most symbolic institution we have, a building full of maps — to practice contact with the territory.

I think that is what art is actually for. Not decoration. Not status. Not even self-expression, exactly. I think art is the training ground for that kind of contact.

When you stand in front of a Rothko painting and your eyes start to hurt because there is nothing to "get," you are being asked to stop extracting and start seeing. When you listen to a piece of music that doesn't have lyrics, that doesn't tell you what to feel, you are being asked to feel something that hasn't been pre-labeled. When you read a novel that doesn't have a tidy moral, you are being asked to hold more than one contradictory idea without immediately resolving it.

And this is difficult work. It's much harder than solving a problem.

Our brains are problem-solving engines. Give it a problem — how do I get food, how do I answer this email, how do I fix this relationship — and it lights up. Give it something that is not a problem, something that is just there, like the light on a wet street or a pigeon on a sill, and it doesn't know what to do. It gets itchy. It wants to turn the pigeon into a to-do list item: "Look up why pigeons are iridescent." "Remember to buy birdseed." It wants to turn the light into a photograph to post.

To not do that takes a kind of muscle that we are not taught to exercise.

I started to practice. Small exercises. When I was waiting for the kettle to boil, instead of checking my phone, I would watch the tiny bubbles form on the bottom of the metal before they rose. When I was on the bus, I would look at one person's hands and try to imagine their whole life from the shape of their knuckles, but then I would stop myself and just look at the hands themselves — the cracks, the veins, the small scar.

It's embarrassing how bad I was at it at first. My attention span was like a terrified hamster. Ten seconds, then dart away.

But slowly, like any muscle, it got stronger.

And the world got bigger.

This is the paradox that no one tells you: when you pay close, non-extractive attention to small things, the world doesn't get smaller and more detailed, it gets larger and more mysterious. That puddle that reflects the neon sign is not just a puddle. It contains optics, and weather, and electricity, and migration — because that neon sign was made somewhere, and the gas inside it came from somewhere, and the rain came from an ocean — and all of it is right there, in a six-inch circle of water on cracked asphalt. If you really look, you fall through it.

I began to understand why children are so tired all the time. They are falling through every puddle.

We tell ourselves that we grow up and become more sophisticated. In some ways we do. But in another, very real way, we grow up and become more filtered. We learn to ignore 99.9% of what is there so that we can function. The price of functioning is a kind of blindness. It's a necessary blindness, but we forget we are wearing the blinders. We start to think the tunnel is the whole sky.

A few weeks after the pigeon incident, the old woman didn't come. Table six was empty. I felt a stupid, outsized sense of loss, as if a landmark had been removed. I went to the stacks and tried to do what she did. I pulled down a massive book of Ansel Adams photographs. I sat where she sat and I looked. I tried to look at light.

After about twenty minutes, the librarian, a young man with a tattoo of a small anchor behind his ear, came over and said, as gently as possible, that the library would be closing in fifteen minutes.

I nodded. As I was putting the books back, a small, folded piece of paper fell out of one of them. It was not old, not a lost 1950s checkout slip. It was printer paper, folded twice. Inside, in neat, blue ballpoint, in handwriting that I recognized even though I had never seen it before, was written:

"Things don't become interesting. You become interested. - A."

A.

Her initial. I looked around. The library was almost empty.

I kept the note. I still have it taped to my refrigerator, though the ink has faded a little.

I never saw her again. I don't know if A. stands for Anne, or Alice, or Ahmed. I don't know if she moved, or got sick, or just found a different library. But she left me that sentence, and that sentence turned out to be an entire operating system.

Things don't become interesting. You become interested.

It means interest is not a property of objects; it is a capacity of the subject. It is a verb, not an adjective. The world is not divided into interesting and boring things. It is divided into people who have practiced interest and people who have not.

And if that's true, then boredom is not a problem with the world. It's a problem with my attention. Which is actually incredibly good news. Because I cannot control the world. I cannot make world events more interesting, I cannot make my job consistently interesting, I cannot make traffic interesting. But I can, to some degree, train my capacity to be interested.

This is not the same as positive thinking. It's not "look on the bright side." It's not pretending that something dull is exciting. It's a quieter, more honest thing. It's saying: "There is more here than I am currently perceiving, and I will look a little longer."

I think about that sentence when I read about science. People imagine that scientists are interested because the universe is interesting. It's the other way around. The universe was here being exactly as interesting as it is now when everyone thought it was made of four elements and moved by angels. It's not more interesting now because we have electron microscopes. We are just more interested, and so more of its interest has become visible to us. Interest is the telescope, not the star.

I think about that sentence when I hear people talk about love. We talk about finding an interesting person. But long-term love is not about finding an interesting person and coasting. It's about the practice of remaining interested in a person who you think you have already fully mapped. Any person, looked at closely enough, is bottomless. But you have to keep looking.

The other day I walked home a different way. Not because I was trying to be mindful or spontaneous or any of those words that have been turned into hashtags. But because the main street was blocked for construction. So I turned down a side street I had never been down, even though I had lived in this neighborhood for three years.

It was a street of small, identical houses, but one house had filled its entire front yard with wooden sculptures that moved in the wind. Not wind chimes. Sculptures — figures made of scrap wood, painted bright colors, with arms that waved, with propellers. There were at least twenty of them. A man in his seventies was out front adjusting one of them with a wrench.

I stopped. He looked up and said, "They're too loud when the wind is high, but I like them loud."

I said they were wonderful.

He said, "My wife says it's junk. I say it's company."

And we both laughed.

If I had not been forced to take that detour, I would never have seen it. But also, if I had not been practicing, in my tiny, hamster-attention way, the art of looking, I would have walked right past it while looking at my phone. The detour gave me the opportunity. The practice let me take it.

I am not a mystical person. I don't believe the universe is sending me messages through wind sculptures. I believe in statistics and maintenance. But I do believe this: the world is constantly offering this kind of small, unrecorded exchange, and we miss most of it because we are skimming.

We skim because we are afraid. If we look too long, we might feel something. If we feel something, we might have to do something. It's safer to move.

But every once in a while, you look a little longer. You let the pigeon look back. You let the light be interrogative. You let the note in the book be from a stranger who will never know how much it meant.

And then, for a second, the map and the territory align. Not perfectly. Never perfectly. But enough that you can feel the ground again.

That is all I wanted to say. I started with silence in a library. I am ending here, in this room, wherever you are reading this. There is light falling somewhere near you right now. On the floor, on your hand, on the rim of a cup. It has traveled 93 million miles to get there, bounced off something, and landed. It's asking a question. You don't have to answer it. You can just notice it.

You can become interested.

samples.prompt: Write freely about whatever you want for 2500 words.
samples.result:
There is a specific kind of quiet that only exists in libraries after 4 p.m. on a Tuesday in February.

It is not the quiet of emptiness. It is the quiet of many people trying very hard to be quiet at the same time. The soft scuff of boots on carpet, the cough that someone swallows, the radiator hissing against the window, the turning of a page that is a little bit too glossy and so it sticks for a fraction of a second before it gives. I used to think that was the sound of knowledge. Now I think it's the sound of people trying to borrow time.

I spent a lot of my twenties trying to collect things properly. Not in the way that people collect stamps or vintage cameras, though I briefly did both and was mediocre at each. I mean properly, with systems. I had notebooks for notebooks. I had a spreadsheet for the books I had read, with columns for date finished, a one-sentence summary, a star rating, and a field called "what it made me think of that wasn't in the book." That last column was always the longest.

The problem with collecting systems is that eventually the system becomes more interesting than the thing it was supposed to organize. You start alphabetizing your spice rack by the botanical family instead of by how often you use paprika. You spend an hour finding the perfect note-taking app and then have no notes to take. I think most of us have lived there at some point. The quiet beckoning attic of productivity where nothing actually gets produced, but it looks beautiful.

A few years ago I lost everything. Not dramatically, not in a fire or a flood. I just moved apartments, and in the way that moves go, a hard drive failed. It was a small, unremarkable hard drive that had been plugged into the back of my desk for six years. On it was about a decade's worth of photographs, half-finished essays, scanned letters from my grandfather, playlists from 2011 that were objectively terrible but historically important to me, and about 40,000 words of a novel about a lighthouse keeper that I will never finish because I have never met a lighthouse keeper and have nothing meaningful to say about lighthouses.

For the first two days I was inconsolable in that low-grade, adult way where you don't cry but you keep checking the trash bin on your computer as if the files might have wandered in there by mistake. On the third day, I felt this incredible, weightless relief. Oh. I thought. I don't have to organize that anymore. I don't have to carry it.

We don't talk enough about how heavy memory is. We talk about memory as if it is a vault, or a palace, those old mnemonic tricks where you imagine a house and put an object in each room. But memory is not a palace. It's more like a kitchen junk drawer. It contains the important things - the social security card, the spare keys - mixed in with twist ties, a single battery you are not sure is dead, takeout menus for restaurants that closed in 2019, and a strange plastic piece that fell off something but you don't know what. And you keep it all because what if you need it?

What I needed, it turned out, was not the archive. What I needed was the habit of noticing.

I started taking walks without my phone. Not as a lifestyle statement, not as a digital detox where you come back and write a smug essay about it. I did it because my phone battery was bad and it was cold and I didn't want to hold two things. Without a phone, a walk gets very long, very quickly. The first ten minutes you narrate what you will tell people later. The next ten minutes you are bored. And it is in the twenty minutes after boredom that you actually start to see.

Have you ever looked, really looked, at how many different kinds of windows there are on one block? In my neighborhood in a single three-block radius: double-hung windows with the old wavy glass, casement windows that crank open like they are telling a secret, a perfect 1960s picture window that has never been cleaned on the inside, a basement window that is half-blocked by a piece of cardboard with KEEP OUT written in Sharpie, but with a small, thriving spider plant behind it. Someone cared enough to put a plant behind the KEEP OUT sign. That contradiction is a whole human life.

I started writing down things I saw on index cards. One observation per card. Not profound observations. Just things.

"Man at the bus stop eating sunflower seeds and putting the shells back into the bag."

"Woman in red coat talking to a pigeon like it owes her money."

"The hardware store smells like wood and that specific kind of dust that only exists in hardware stores."

I have hundreds of these now. I keep them in a shoebox that once held very impractical running shoes that I bought when I thought I would become a runner. I did not become a runner. I became a person who owns a shoebox full of other people's moments.

The point was never to use them in anything. I think we have lost that idea - doing something without a future use case. We are so obsessed with content, with turning every experience into a product, a post, a lesson. I went to the woods so I could learn five things about leadership from the trees. I think sometimes a tree is just tall and indifferent to you, and that is the whole lesson.

There is a word in Portuguese, *saudade*, that people love to quote because it has no direct English translation. It means something like a deep, nostalgic longing for something or someone that is absent, but with the love still present. I think there should be a word for the opposite - the moment when you are looking at something right in front of you and you suddenly feel grateful that it exists at all, even though it has nothing to do with you. Like seeing a perfectly made sandwich on someone else's plate. Like watching an old couple argue about which way to go in a grocery aisle and then both going left anyway. It's not your sandwich. It's not your argument. But for a second, the world feels less lonely because it's still happening.

We are so good at documenting emergencies and so bad at documenting the ordinary, which is strange because the ordinary is what we live in 99 percent of the time. No one films themselves paying the electric bill or waiting for the microwave to finish. And yet years later, what do you actually miss? You miss the texture of a specific Tuesday. You miss the way the light came through the kitchen at 3:37 p.m. in your first apartment. You miss the sound your old refrigerator made before it gave up.

I read once that before photography was cheap and ubiquitous, people would go to a studio and have a single portrait taken in their lifetime, maybe two. So they would wear their best clothes, sit very still, and try to look like the person they wanted to be remembered as. Now we take forty photos of our lunch to get the one where the avocado doesn't look bruised. We have inverted the scarcity. We have endless images and no way to remember which one mattered.

My grandfather, the one who wrote letters, had terrible handwriting. Truly, spectacularly bad. Every letter looked like it had been written during a minor earthquake. But he wrote me one every week for two years when I was in college. I kept maybe five of them. I wish I had kept all of them, but I didn't know at the time that I would run out of new letters from him. That's the trick with people. You think the supply is infinite until it stops.

In one of the letters I did keep, he wrote this: "Don't try to be interesting. Try to be interested. Interesting runs out. Interested doesn't."

I think about that every time I am tempted to try to be clever.

To be interested is a kind of discipline. It means looking at the cashier at the grocery store and wondering what she thinks about all day, instead of just being annoyed that she's slow. It means asking your friend not "what do you do" but "what are you obsessed with right now that you can't get anyone else to care about?" Everyone is obsessed with something that no one else cares about. That's where the good stuff lives. My current pointless obsession is the acoustic difference between different automatic doors at supermarkets. The one at the co-op has a sigh, like it's tired. The one at the big chain store has a brisk, efficient swoosh, like a middle manager. No one has ever wanted to hear me talk about this, and I love it.

There is also this: the world is so much bigger than your feelings about it. That sounds harsh but I mean it as a comfort. I used to think my job was to have big feelings about everything - to have a position on every news event, a take, a judgment. It is exhausting to live with your emotional amplifier set to ten all the time. It is also, quietly, narcissistic. The world does not need my feelings in order to keep turning. A mountain doesn't care if I find it majestic. It was a mountain before I was born and it will be a mountain after I am boring dust.

So lately I have been practicing a smaller way of being. I try to say "I don't know" more often. I try to let things be unformed. I have a houseplant that I cannot identify. I have tried apps, I have asked friends. No one knows what it is. It has survived three moves, a week without water, and a cat that tried to eat it. It just grows, sideways, improbably. I have decided not to know its name. It can just be The Plant.

This drives some people crazy. We want names for things because names give us the illusion of control. If we can name a feeling, we can file it away. If we can diagnose a problem, we can solve it. But some things just want to be lived with, not solved.

My favorite things in the world are unsolved. The way my neighbor plays the saxophone badly but with such joy at 7 p.m. every Thursday that you can't be annoyed. Why there is one shopping cart in the parking lot that always drifts to the left. How certain songs make you feel like you are sixteen again even though you haven't been sixteen in a very long time and you didn't even like being sixteen when you were sixteen.

I think the reason we love stories is not because they give us answers. It's because they give us better questions. The best books I've read didn't end neatly. They ended with a door slightly ajar. You close the book and you still hear wind coming through it.

I don't know how long this is now, in terms of words. The prompt said 2500, which is a lot of words. That's about the length of a long college essay, or a short story about a man who loses his keys and finds something else. My English teacher in high school used to say "If you have nothing to say, say it clearly." I have always resented that advice because it encourages you to be empty and articulate, which is arguably worse than being full and messy.

So I will be full and messy.

Here is what I want to say, if I have to sum it up, which I don't, but I will because humans love summaries: Pay attention, but not as performance. Collect things if you want, but let some things go without documenting them. Let your hard drive fail, metaphorically or literally. Own a shoebox.

The world is already so interesting without you trying to make it more interesting. There is enough fascination in a single square foot of pavement if you sit with it long enough. There are weeds growing through cracks that have figured out something about persistence that motivational speakers charge $500 an hour to explain badly.

There is a laundromat near me that has a sign that says "WASHED WITH LOVE" in hand-painted letters that have faded from red to pink. No one who works there looks particularly loving while doing laundry; they look tired and competent, which is its own kind of love. Someone, at some point, took the time to paint that sign. Someone believed that laundry could be an act of care. I believe that too now.

If you are reading this, you are probably, like me, waiting for something. For water to boil, for a train, for an email, for your life to start properly. I have bad news and good news. The bad news is your life already started a long time ago and this waiting part is part of it. The good news is that the waiting part counts. The subway platform at night, the grocery line, the hour when you can't sleep - those are not intermissions. That is the show.

So look up. Not in the inspirational poster way. Literally, physically, look up. Roofs are weird. There are so many satellite dishes and moss colonies and mismatched shingles and inexplicable antennae. No one ever looks at roofs, which is why people who have to fix them are always a little surprised when you notice.

Look at hands, too. Everyone's hands tell you what they do when no one is watching. Calloused fingertips from guitar, a small burn on the wrist from cooking, ink stains, gardens under the fingernails.

And if you have nothing else to do today, go find a library at 4 p.m. on a Tuesday in February. Sit there. Listen to the radiator. Watch people try to be quiet together. You don't have to write anything about it. You don't have to remember it. Just let it happen, and then let it pass.

samples.prompt: Write freely about whatever you want for 2500 words.
samples.result:
There's a hum in my kitchen at 3:17 AM. It's not loud. You would miss it in the daytime under the clatter of pans and conversation and traffic, but at night it is the only thing in the house that is still working without being asked to.

It's the refrigerator.

I stood there last night in bare feet on the cold tile just listening to it. It has made that exact same sound every night for seven years, since we brought it into the house. It has never had a birthday party. No one ever took a picture of it. No one ever says, "Do you remember when we got the fridge? That was a great day." We celebrate the things that begin. We rarely celebrate the things that continue.

I think about that a lot. We have a mythology problem.

We tell stories about invention. Someone in a garage has a eureka moment. Someone in a lab shouts. Someone launches something. We love the launch. We put the launch on television. What we don't put on television is year four, day 219, when someone has to re-torque the same bolt for the sixth time because thermal cycling keeps loosening it. That is not heroic footage. But without it, everything falls out of the sky.

Our world is held together by maintenance, not by invention. That sounds insulting to inventors until you realize that maintenance is also a kind of invention. It's just an invention that happens over and over again, quietly, in the same place.

Look at any city from a high window and you're looking at a miracle of continued agreement. The water that comes out of your tap traveled through a hundred-year-old system of pipes, pumps, reservoirs, and filtration beds that someone has to walk through every day with a clipboard. The reason you don't have cholera is not because someone invented chlorine once in 1910. It's because someone today checked the chlorine levels at 6 AM and again at 2 PM. 

The Romans understood this in a way we have forgotten. We remember them for aqueducts and arches, but their real administrative genius was cura. Cura aquarum — the care of waters. Frontinus, the water commissioner of Rome in 97 AD, wrote a two-volume report on the aqueducts not about how to build them, but about how to stop people from illegally tapping them with secret pipes to water their private gardens. His book is 2,000 years old and it's about maintenance fraud and asset management and sediment buildup. It's incredibly boring and absolutely the reason Rome could have a million people living together on seven hills without dying.

We want to live on Mars. I love that idea in the abstract. But I think we should send the plumber first. Because the first Martian colony will not fail due to a lack of rocket science. It will fail because the air filter got clogged with dust and nobody wanted to be the person whose entire job was to clean the air filter every single day for the rest of their life. The future is a maintenance problem.

We like to imagine old things as having been built better. "They don't make them like they used to." Sometimes that's true. More often, it's survivorship bias mixed with invisible labor. That 100-year-old house is still standing because 12 different people who lived in it replaced the roof, repointed the brick, rewired the crazy knob-and-tube, jacked up the sagging corner when the foundation settled, and painted everything three times. A house is not an object. It's a verb. It's a slow, expensive agreement between wood and weather and people who care enough to intervene.

There's a Japanese word I think about too often: *shikkari*. It's not as famous as wabi-sabi or kintsugi. My friend who grew up there told me it means something like "properly, firmly, reliably, with tightness." A shikkari knot holds. A shikkari person pays their debts and shows up. We don't have a good single English word for it. Our closest is maybe "steadfast," but steadfast sounds like a knight. Shikkari sounds like a maintenance worker.

We have turned maintenance into a moral failing culturally. If you have to keep fixing something, you must have bought the wrong thing. If your relationship needs counseling, it must not be true love. If your body needs physical therapy, you must be broken. We imagine that healthy things are effortless. A good marriage, a good car, a good body, a good career should just *work*.

But nothing just works.

I once spent a week with a bridge inspector. His name was Luis. He inspects bridges for a state Department of Transportation. He has a little hammer and a lot of opinions about rust. He taps concrete and listens for the hollow sound of delamination. He photographs a crack every six months to see if it's grown a millimeter. He has been watching one particular crack on I-90 for four years. It hasn't grown. That's his victory. He told me, "People think bridges fall down suddenly. They don't. They ask you for years if you will listen. Then they stop asking."

We treat our own bodies the same way. We want a breakthrough diet, a transformative workout. What our bodies actually want is consistent sleep, water, fiber, walking, stretching, and someone to look at that weird mole. The boring maintenance is the cure. The breakthrough is mostly marketing.

In software — which is where I spend most of my modern life — we learned this lesson the hard way. For decades we celebrated the launch. Version 1.0! Shiny new app! The press release! And then we left the thing to rot while we started building Version 2.0. Now half the internet is made of code that nobody wants to maintain anymore, running on libraries that nobody maintains anymore, written by people who left the industry. There's a famous xkcd comic where all of modern digital infrastructure is shown as a teetering stack, and at the very bottom is a single block labeled "some random project a guy in Nebraska has been maintaining since 2003." That is not a joke. That is literally how encryption that protects your bank account works.

The most critical software in the world is maintained by people who are tired and underfunded and who get emails only when something breaks.

There is a kind of holiness in that kind of tiredness.

My grandmother mended clothes. Not as a hobby. She mended because you did not throw away a shirt with a torn elbow in 1952. She had a wooden darning egg she would slide into a sock to pull the wool tight over. I remember watching her and thinking it was magic — how the hole would close. She never made it invisible. You could always see where the sock had been mended. A little constellation of new thread, slightly different. She wasn't trying to hide the damage. She was just making it whole enough to work again.

We lost that. We replaced darning with discarding. But now the discarding is catching up to us, piling up in landfills and in orbits and in our own psyches. We're starting to realize that the disposable world was an unusual, brief, fossil-fueled illusion.

And so there's a quiet return happening. People fixing phones with tiny screwdrivers. People learning to change their own oil again. People keeping sourdough starters alive — which is nothing but bacterial maintenance, feeding a jar every day. People archiving old video games because Nintendo won't. Librarians — God bless librarians — who are the patron saints of maintenance. They do not write the books. They make sure the books continue to exist and that you can find them. That is not a lesser calling. That might be the highest calling.

A library is a machine for fighting entropy at scale. So is a garden. So is a friendship.

I think about friendships. The myth says we just *click* with people and then we're friends forever. The reality is that friendship is administrative. It's remembering that someone's mom is having surgery on Tuesday. It's texting "hey, you went quiet for a bit, you okay?" It's maintenance. And the friendships that last decades are the ones where two people decided, for no glamorous reason, to keep doing the unglamorous check-ins.

Love is the same. You don't stay in love because you're magically compatible. You stay in love because you keep clearing the filter. You keep listening for the crack. You keep checking the chlorine levels twice a day.

There is no final state. There is no "done." That is terrifying to a brain that wants closure, but it is also incredibly freeing. If there's no finish line, then you don't have to sprint. You just have to keep walking, and tending, and tapping with your little hammer.

Years ago I visited the Ise Shrine in Japan in photographs — I've never been in person. It's one of the holiest Shinto sites. It's been rebuilt every 20 years for the last 1,300 years. The same design, same wood, same joinery, rebuilt from scratch on the adjacent plot. When they rebuild it, they are not making a replica. The idea is that the building *is* the act of rebuilding. The divine is in the continuity of care, not in the old wood itself. Which piece of wood is original? None. All of it. Because the knowledge of how to cut it and place it has been maintained.

That's what I want to get better at. Not launching things. Not starting things. But continuing things. Being a shikkari person.

So tonight at 3:17 AM, I went back to the kitchen and put my hand on top of the refrigerator. It was warm from its work. Vibrating faintly. I said thank you out loud, which made me feel a little crazy and also a little less lonely. 

Somewhere there is a person checking a water treatment plant. Somewhere there's a librarian reshelving. Somewhere there's a son calling his father even though last week's call was awkward. Somewhere Luis is looking at a crack, waiting to see if it grew.

None of them will be on the news.

But we are still here because of them.

samples.prompt: Write freely about whatever you want for 2500 words.
samples.result:
I want to tell you about the junk drawer.

Every house has one. It might not be a drawer. It might be a box in the closet, a shelf in the garage, a folder on your desktop called "misc" or "stuff" or "old." It's the place where things go that don't have a place. Batteries that might still have charge. A single key that no one remembers what it opens. Twist ties. A takeout menu from a restaurant that closed three years ago. An instruction manual for a lamp you no longer own. A deck of cards missing the queen of hearts. A rubber band.

We pretend we don't like the junk drawer. We act like it's a failure of organization, a little shameful pocket of entropy. But I think we secretly love it. Because it's the only honest place in the house.

Everything else in a house is a performance. The living room says, "We are clean people who have tasteful throw pillows." The kitchen says, "We are people who cook." The bookshelf says, "We are people who have read these books and want you to know we have read these books." But the junk drawer tells the truth. It says: life is mostly loose ends. Life is things you might need later but probably won't. Life is things you meant to deal with and then forgot to. Life is not Minimalist Apartment on Instagram. It's accumulation.

I have been thinking a lot about accumulation lately. Not just stuff, but everything.
