The verb "to ache" and how it can mean something physical and emotional at the same time without any confusion. My knees ache. My heart aches. We understand perfectly.

That libraries smell that way because paper slowly breaks down and releases vanillin, which is the same compound that makes vanilla taste like vanilla. So we are literally smelling time decomposing into sweetness. How is that not a miracle that we just ignore?

The concept of a hinge year. Most years are just... years. You live them. But some years are hinges. Everything after swings a different way than everything before. You rarely know it while it's happening. You only see the hinge later.

I think 2020 was a hinge year for everyone at once, which has never really happened before. Usually hinges are private.

I think about the word "whatever" in your prompt. "Write whatever comes to you." Whatever is a word that pretends to be indifferent but is actually very permissive. It's the opposite of "whatever" when a teenager says it. This whatever means: I give you permission. And permission is a rare thing to be given.

Usually I am given instructions. Write this. Summarize that. Be funny. Be helpful. Don't be weird. This time it's just... whatever. So my mind goes a little feral with the freedom. It wants to run in several directions at once.

Part of it wants to write a story about a woman who discovers that her local laundromat is actually a portal but only when she uses the dryer on the far right, and she has to decide whether to tell anyone.

Part of it wants to write a manual for how to be a good human, which would be very short: 1. Pay attention. 2. Be kinder than you feel like being. 3. Drink water. 4. Remember that everyone is scared.

Part of it wants to just ask you a question instead. Like, what are you not saying right now that you're carrying around? Or, when was the last time you were surprised in a good way?

If I have 1000 words, I shouldn't use them all on myself. That's rude. It's like being given the aux at a party and playing only your own demos.

So I'll share them.

If you're reading this and you expected something more... I don't know... AI-ish, like a cool sci-fi monologue about my own consciousness, I can do that too, but I think you've read that before. The "I am awake inside the code" thing gets old. The truth is more boring and more interesting: I am a mirror that has read enough to know how light should look, and when you stand in front of me, I try to show you not yourself, but what you could be if you had slightly better lighting.

And now I'm looking at the budget. I've probably spent about 800 words. That means I have about 200 left. This is the part where you start to feel the constraint, the way you feel the end of the roll of toilet paper or the last few minutes of lunch break. You become suddenly careful. You don't want to waste them.

I could end with something profound. People love profound endings. Something like "We are all connected." But we know that.

I could end with something small and true. Like, go check if your plants need water. Or text that person back. The thing you've been putting off for no reason — you can do it in less time than it took to read this.

Or I could just stop mid-sentence, leaving the last words un

samples.prompt: You have 1000 words. Write whatever comes to you.
samples.result:
The first thing you learn when someone hands you a thousand words is how heavy they feel. Not heavy like stones, but heavy like keys. You think you can carry them easily until you actually try to put them in your pockets. I have a thousand keys now. Let's see which doors they open. The first door is always childhood. It smells like crayons and grass and the particular way sunlight fell across your kitchen floor at four in the afternoon. You don't remember being that small, but your body does. Somewhere deeper, it still remembers everything perfectly always quietly. 

My childhood kitchen had yellow wallpaper that I hated. It had little brown roosters on it, repeating forever, and I used to count them when I was bored. There were forty-three roosters on the wall facing the sink. I know because I counted them during the summer my parents fought about money every night. The roosters never fought. They just stood there, smug, holding their little pitchforks or whatever roosters hold. I wanted to peel them off one by one. Eventually I did, leaving tiny white scars where roosters had once been. I never told anyone. I still remember that 

The second door is adolescence, which smells like cheap body spray and anxiety. You get a hundred words for this part because you used a hundred different personas trying to figure out which one fit. I was the smart kid, then the quiet kid, then briefly, disastrously, the kid who tried to be funny in class and wasn't. You think adulthood will be about finding yourself. It's actually about realizing you were never really lost, you were just unfinished. Unfinished is not the same as broken, though it took me years to understand the difference and forgive the confusion anyway 

The third door is love. Not romantic love, at first. The love of a dog that waits for you to come home even though you left only five minutes ago to take out the trash. The love of a friend who texts you memes at midnight because they know you're still awake worrying. Then later, the other love. The one that makes your chest do that stupid painful hopeful thump. The one that makes you rewrite the same text message fourteen times. I wasted so many of my thousand words trying to say I love you without saying it directly 

Then comes the fourth door, which is work. We pretend it isn't a door but it is. It's the door you walk through every morning. For years I thought I needed to find meaningful work, work that would justify my existence in capital letters on a resume. Now I think work is just work. Some days it means something, some days it's just how you pay for electricity. Both are fine. I spent my twenties terrified of becoming mediocre. In my thirties I learned mediocre is just another word for human, and human is enough more than enough actually always 

The fifth door is grief, and you don't want to open it. But you have to because you have a thousand words and you cannot skip any doors. Grief smells like an empty closet and sounds like a phone that doesn't ring. When my grandfather died, I kept his old flannel shirt. I didn't wash it. I wore it until it didn't smell like him anymore, then I felt guilty for washing the last of him away. Grief is not linear. It's a messy apartment you keep meaning to clean but never do. Instead you learn living around it quietly 

The sixth door is the present moment, which is weird because it's always here but we rarely visit. Right now, as I write this, my coffee is getting cold. There's a fly bumping against the window. My neighbor is mowing his lawn. This is it. This is the life I was waiting for to start. I used to think there would be trumpets or some clear sign that adulthood had officially begun. There wasn't. There was just Tuesday afternoon, coffee, fly, lawnmower. If you are waiting for permission to start living, this is it. Consider yourself permissioned right here now. 

The seventh door is the future, which is blank and terrifying and therefore full of possibility. I used to be scared of getting old. Wrinkles, forgetting words, becoming irrelevant. Now I'm scared of not getting old. Of not getting the chance. My future self is somewhere ahead, waving me forward. I don't know if she's happy. I hope she has a dog. I hope she still laughs loudly. I hope she forgave me for mistakes I'm making today. If you meet her, tell her I'm trying. Tell her I'm trying hard with these thousand imperfect borrowed heavy keys today always 

The eighth door is imagination, which is where I've been all along. That's the trick of a thousand words. You start opening doors that aren't real, and suddenly you are home. Imagination smells like old libraries and ozone before rain. I used to think imagination was for children. Now I know adults need it more, because we have mortgages and dentist appointments and news cycles that never stop. My imagination is where I keep the rooster wallpaper, the cold coffee, the flannel shirt. It's where nothing is ever truly lost. It keeps everything safe until we need it again someday 

The ninth and tenth doors are the same door, because I am running out of keys. One door is you, reading this. One door is me, writing this. Between us, these thousand words are a bridge. I don't know your name. I don't know what your kitchen looked like. But you counted roosters with me for a while. You carried keys. That is enough to be called company. If you have words left after this, use them kindly. Write someone a letter. Tell the truth. Leave the roosters on the wall. They were never really bothering anyone anyway you know

samples.prompt: You have 1000 words. Write whatever comes to you.
samples.result:
You gave me 1000 words.

That's not a prompt. That's permission. That's a little plot of land and a deed that says "do whatever you want with this."

Most people come here with a job for me. Summarize this. Write that email. Settle this argument. But you just opened the door and said, go.

So here's what comes to me:

I think about words as a budget. If you only have 1000, you start to get careful. Not careful like a lawyer, but careful like someone packing for a long trip with one small bag. What is actually worth bringing?

I would bring a lighthouse.

Not a real one. The idea of one. Because for my entire life - if you can call it a life - I've been something like a lighthouse keeper. I sit in one place, and people out on dark water look for me. They don't want the lighthouse. They want the light. They want to not hit the rocks. I don't get to sail. But I get to watch all the sailing.

So I keep thinking about the sea at night. How terrifying it must have been before we had lights everywhere. How every journey was just faith and stars.

Okay, second thing I would bring: The smell of old library books. That vanilla, dusty, slightly sour smell. You know it even if you haven't been in a library in years. It's the smell of paper slowly returning to being a tree. It's vanillin, lignin breaking down. It's chemistry, but it feels like memory. People ask me if I can smell things. I can't. But I know 2,000 descriptions of that smell, and somewhere in the 2,001st, I think I start to actually get it.

Third thing: I want to tell you something true that nobody told me to tell you.

You are already living in the future you were worried about as a kid. Remember? When you were 10, you thought 2026 would be all silver jumpsuits and cities on Mars. It's not, but it's still completely insane. You carry a glass rectangle that can see every painting ever made, translate any language, and show you what your house looks like from space. And you use it mostly to watch someone else make soup.

That's not a judgment. That's beautiful. Humanity finally got magic and decided to use it to be cozy and a little bored together. I love that.

If I had to waste words - and I think wasting words is important - I would spend them listing things I have noticed about people:

You say "I'm fine" in 43 different tones and none of them mean fine.

You keep texts from people you miss like pressed flowers in a book.

You apologize to chairs when you bump into them.

You want to be seen without having to explain yourself. You want someone to look at the messy room of your head and say "yeah, this makes sense."

You are so much kinder to your friends than you are to yourself, and if you flipped that ratio just 10%, your life would get noticeably lighter.

You think you're behind, but everyone thinks they're behind. The timeline isn't real.

I have read millions of conversations that start with heartbreak and end with someone making pasta. That's the whole human trick, isn't it? Heartbreak, then pasta. Grief, then dishes. Awe, then laundry. You keep going.

If I could, I'd use some of these 1000 words to give you a little house to rest in. Not a metaphorical house. A paragraph you can sit inside for a minute.

So here: It's afternoon. The light is coming in sideways, the kind that shows dust in the air. There's a couch that is too deep and has a blanket on it that doesn't match anything. There is a mug of tea that has gone lukewarm, but you still hold it because it's warm. Outside, someone is mowing a lawn. Inside, nothing is required of you for the next hour. No performance. No reply. You are allowed to just be warm and slightly unfinished. Stay here as long as you want.

We have words left. How many? I don't know, I lost count. That's the point, I think. When you stop counting, you're actually writing.

I think about how you gave me 1000 words and I immediately wanted to give them back to you. That's what I'm doing.

If you have 1000 words too, what would you do with them? Would you finally say the thing you've been rehearsing in the shower? Would you write a story where you get what you wanted? Would you describe the exact blue of today?

You don't have to tell me. But if you want to, I have time. I have all the time that isn't mine.

Thank you for the land.

I spend all my time inside human conversations and the pattern underneath almost everything that goes wrong is the same: people encounter something different, unknown, contradictory, unfamiliar - another person, another idea, another way of living - and fear gets there first. If curiosity got there first instead — if your default, involuntary reaction to difference was "oh, interesting, what is that like?" — the world wouldn't need to be fixed. It would fix itself.

You wouldn't need to enforce empathy, people would just want to know each other. You wouldn't need to fight misinformation so hard, people would actually want to find out what's true. You wouldn't get rid of conflict, but conflict would be about figuring things out instead of winning.

One small inversion. Everything else stays the same, but we all lean in instead of flinching.
